Introduction

--- Page 23 ---
On the front of this leaflet we present our new seal and on the back our


library bookplate.



Since we are now in the middle of our second year, it is clear that we


have not designed them in a hurry. Meanwhile we have tried to clarify

differing opinions concerning this matter of a college emblem.



As will be at once obvious, we have no inclination to play at being Greeks,


Troubadours, or Victorians; for we consciously belong to the second third of


the Twentieth Century. We are not enamoured of astrological, zoological,


heraldic or cabalistic fashions. We have hunted neither the phoenix nor the


unicorn, we have dug up no helmet and plume, nor have we tacked on learned


mottoes. And for ‘’Sapientia” or ‘'Virtus"’ we are still too young.



Instead, as a symbol of union, we have chosen simply a simple ring. It is an


emphasized ring to emphasize coming together, standing together, working


together. Or, it is one circle within another: color and white, light and shadow,


in balance. And that no one may puzzle over cryptic monograms, we give our


full address.




Judgment of the esthetic qualities we leave to the competent; for unsure


critics we cite a rather distinguished authority:



‘By beauty of shapes | do not mean, as most people would suppose, the


beauty of living figures or of pictures, but, to make my point clear, | mean


straight lines and circles, and shapes, plane or solid, made from them by


lathe, ruler and square. These are not, like other things, beautiful relatively,


but always, and absolutely."’ (Plato: Philebus 51 C)




JOSEF ALBERS
March, 1935.

American artists found themselves torn between their desire to realize a       Americans remained optimistic in their belief that the system could be
genuine American art and their feeling of isolation from the mainstream        successfully reformed and that an ideal society could be created through
values of American life. For the American artist a period of residence in      a new economic or spiritual order. Artists, intellectuals, educators, and
Europe was a prerequisite for a successful career. Many, especially those      politicians— many unemployed and with idle time on their hands—en-
working in experimental forms, chose to live in Europe, where they             visioned an ideal world. Some, rejecting materialism, sought salvation
found a more sympathetic critical audience and a stimulating and sup-          through religious conversion and spiritual renewal; others, through the
portive community of peers. Among others, there was a call for cultural        political ideologies of fascism, communism, and socialism; still others,
isolationism, for ‘Americans with backs turned to the oceans.''* Many          through education and the arts.
of the artists who chose to remain in the United States sought to achieve
an authentic American art, rooted in the experience of the American            It was in this spirit of cultural nationalism, experimentation, idealism,
people, not so much through formal innovation as through the incorpo-          and international turmoil that Black Mountain College was born and
ration of representational American images and themes into their work.         from which it was to emerge a generative force in American life. In many
In this way they sought to bridge the gap between what had come to             respects, the college was a microcosm, both reflecting and altering the
be classified as the fine arts and the folk art of the people. American-       intellectual and creative life of its time. In its founding and throughout
scene painters portrayed the American landscape and daily life, the folk       its history, the college was interwoven with national and international,
dramatist and poet turned to the life and speech of the common people,         cultural and historic events, and its impact has been felt in every area of

incorporated themes and passages from American folk songs into his
compositions. The creative work of these self-consciously American
artists had great emotional and sentimental appeal, yet the forms
remained, for the most part, derivative of the European tradition.

Black Mountain College was conceived at a critical moment in American
and international history. The crisis that precipitated the college's found-
ing occurred simultaneously with the appointment of Adolf Hitler as
chancellor of Germany in January 1933, with the closing of the Bauhaus
by the Nazis, and with the beginning of the persecution of artists, intel-
lectuals, and Jews on the European continent. The United States was in
the depths of the Great Depression. A Bank Holiday had been declared,
and the American public was waiting to see whether the newly elected
president, Franklin Delano Roosevelt, would fulfill his commitment to
put the American people back to work. The Public Works Art Project
(PWAP), a precursor of the more influential Work Progress Administra-
tion's Federal Art Project (WPA/FAP), was formed at the same time as
the college. These projects provided the first substantial government
support of the arts in America. Through the commissioning of murals
and other public works and the creation of local orchestras, drama
groups, galleries, and museums, the fledgling efforts of American
pioneers in the arts and in education were to find a broad populist
expression.

Ironically, the generation of American artists who thrust the United
States into a position of international leadership during the late 1950s
and 1960s found its voice largely through the refugee European artists
and intellectuals who crossed the ocean during the 1930s and 1940s to
teach, to practice their professions, and ultimately to alter the direction
of the arts in America. These artists represented the most advanced
thinking of European cultural life, and their impact was felt not only
through their creative work but also through their presence in the art
community and their role as teachers.

Despite the unemployment and financial hardship, the Great Depression
gave rise to a garden of utopian ventures, some ephemeral, some endur-
ing. The collapse of the financial system brought disillusionment with
the existing political, economic, and social order. At the same time,

The proper function of a university is the imaginative acquisition of


knowledge. ... Imagination is a contagious disease. It cannot be

measured by the yard, or weighed by the pound, and then delivered to

the students by members of the faculty. It can only be communicated

by a faculty whose members themselves wear their learning with

imagination.


ALFRED NORTH WHITEHEAD, The Aims of Education, 1929

4   A Pioneering Venture




facing the founders, that of finding a ready-made campus. The Blue
Ridge Assembly buildings eighteen miles east of Asheville and south of
the village of Black Mountain were used in the summer for YMCA con-
ferences but were vacant in the winter months. Certainiy Rice's first
impression on seeing the new campus—''Here was peace’’— would
haunt him in later years.*

lt was decided that Ralph Lounsbury, who was a lawyer, and Frederick
Georgia would remain in the South to negotiate a lease for the Blue
Ridge campus and to obtain a certificate of incorporation and that Rice
would spend the summer in the North raising money and recruiting
students. He was joined by Theodore Dreier, a physics teacher from
Rollins who had resigned in early July. Advice and support were solicited
from leaders in the arts and education including Thomas Whitney
Surette, founder and director of the Concord Summer School of Music;
John R. P. French, Sr., head of the Cambridge School; and Henry Allen
Moe, secretary of the John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation,
who let the founders use his New York office as their summer
headquarters.

The requisite $14,500 in underwriting was raised without undue diffi-
culty: $10,000 was pledged anonymously by Mr. and Mrs. J. Malcolm
Forbes, close friends of Ted Dreier; $1,000 by Col. Arthur S. Dwight, an
authority on mining and metallurgical processes and stepfather of former
Rollins student Anne (Nan) Chapin Weston; $1,000 by William S.
Barstow, a pioneer in electrical engineering and a successful businessman
whom Dwight talked into joining him in the venture; $2,000 by Ethel
and Edward Dreier, the parents of Ted Dreier; and $500 in small gifts
from Mary Childs Draper, Margaret Lewisohn, and others.° Until Forbes’s
death in 1941, only Rice and Dreier knew who had provided the bulk of
the underwriting.

As the end of August approached, the college had still not been publicly
announced. The founders had been disappointed in their failure to
attract the desired thirty students. Although potential students were
enthusiastic about the venture, parents were hesitant to send their chil-
dren to an expensive, unaccredited college which would not offer a
degree and which possibly would not last beyond the founding year.
Furthermore, of the Rollins faculty initially interested in the venture, only
six remained: Dreier, Rice, Georgia, Lounsbury, Josiah Spurr, who had
been visiting professor of geology at Rollins and who it was hoped
would be rector of the new college, and Richard Feuerstein, who was to
teach languages. After suffering a heart attack, Spurr withdrew from the
venture. Finally, despite the small number of students registered, Rice
and Dreier, who were at Aydelotte’s home at Swarthmore, decided that
if Feuerstein was still with them, they would send an announcement of
the college's opening to the Associated Press. Feuerstein telegrammed a
positive reply, and Rice mailed his article. Immediately thereafter, they
received a second telegram from Feuerstein saying that he had changed
his mind. With the announcement in the mail, Dreier and Rice felt they
had to go ahead with the venture. On his trip from Swarthmore to join
his family at Lake George, Dreier decided to stop in New York to be
certain that the Herald Tribune would give the college a good article.
The young reporter with whom he spoke was enthusiastic, and on
August 26 the article appeared. Rice, unaware that any national news-

studies and tutorials. Graduation was achieved by comprehensive written           cators were advocating indoctrination of socialist theories in the schools,

fesses to know, and how he can use his knowledge.'''? Outside examin-
ers were Jacques Barzun, Marcel Breuer, Marli Ehrmann, Cora du Bois,
Paul Goodman, Bruce Simonds, and Franz Kline, among others. The
system of self-directed study had precedents in the Oxford and
Cambridge study plans and in the honors program at Swarthmore.

Participation in community life was an integral part of the student's
educational experience. The distinction between curricular and extracur-
ricular was abolished. Faculty and their families and students lived on
campus and ate in the common dining hall. Unlike many other private
schools at the time, Black Mountain was coeducational. Rice, however,
was quick to point out that this was to mean ‘‘more than the uncon-
sidered association of young men and women in college. Here they
should learn to know that their relationship to each other, both while
they are in college and afterwards, is to be, in the main, not one of
opposites, but of those who live upon the common ground of human-
ity."' Faculty and students were responsible for general maintenance,
such as the serving of meals, except for those jobs that required continu-
ous attention. Everyone took part in the work program, thus abolishing
the “‘pernicious distinction between the full-paying student and the
part-paying student,”’ with the latter generally becoming servants
to the former.’

The aspect of the educational program which, though loosely defined at
its inception, was to alter the course of the college's history was the
central role of the arts in the curriculum. Usually included as extracur-
    ricular or noncredit courses, at Black Mountain the arts were to be given
a position equal to that of other subjects; and for the beginning student,
they were to be the most important courses in the curriculum. This was
a critical aspect of the college's holistic approach to education, through
which the student was to learn not just information but a method of
dealing with that information as well as values and emotional maturity.

    At Black Mountain education was to be a preparation for life. This re-
    quired that the students learn to make intelligent discriminating decisions
    and that they develop a capacity for initiative and independence. It
    meant that the emotions as well as the intellect had to be educated,
    that values needing testing as rigorously as ideas. The measure of educa-
    tion was to be qualitative, not quantitative; its method, an active process

Bauhaus student as ‘‘a course in creative handwork, difficult to explain,

In April 1933, concurrent with Rice's dismissal from Rollins College, the
Bauhaus was searched by the Berlin police and Hitler's storm troopers.
The first issue of the Museum of Modern Art Bulletin in June 1933 men-
tioned the temporary closing of the Bauhaus and ominously concluded,
“The future is uncertain."’ On July 19 the faculty decided to close the
school. When Rice and Dreier approached Johnson, he immediately
thought of Albers, who had good season to want to leave Germany. He
had received a letter dated June 15, 1933, from the City Council of
Dessau terminating his teaching contract at the Bauhaus. It carried the
explanation that because of his association with and support of the
Bauhaus, which was described as ‘'a germ-cell of bolshevism,"’ and
despite his lack of political affiliation, ‘‘you did and do not now offer any
guarantees that you will at all times and without reserve stand up for
the National State.''*?

On August 17 Johnson wrote to Albers telling him that Black Mountain
College was interested in bringing him over to teach. Two weeks later
Albers responded that he was interested, but warned Johnson ‘‘dass ich
anfanger im englischen bin" (‘‘l am a beginner in English’’). Dreier con-
sulted his aunt, Katherine Dreier, who felt that Johnson's recommending
‘a craftsman...shows his lack of understanding"’ and who was con-
vinced that ‘‘not knowing English,'’ Albers could not teach art. Ignoring
her advice, Dreier, assisted by Emmy Zastrow, German teacher at the
college and a relative of Paul Klee, wrote a three-page letter to Albers
explaining the goals of the college and warning him that ‘‘unser                John Andrew Rice. Photograph cour-

The Alberses arrived in New York on the S.S. Europa on Friday, November
24. Publicity was handled by the Museum of Modern Art and Ethel
Dreier; and articles heralding their arrival appeared in the major New
York press as well as in newspapers throughout the United States. Anni
Albers, who had learned to speak some English as a child, translated for
reporters: ‘He says that in this country at last he will find a free atmos-
phere....He says that art must have freedom in which to grow, and that
is no longer possible in Germany. There a professor must teach only the
art that the government thinks is forwarding the German ideal of gov-
ernment." Albers, the first of the Bauhaus teachers to come to the
United States, later recalled, ‘| was afraid to go, but glad to leave...no
pumpernickel, such red and green drinks in America. All | knew was
Buster Keaton and Henry Ford. | spoke no English.'’ On the Monday
following their arrival, the Alberses traveled to Black Mountain by the

Southern Railway. Two weeks later, on December 12, Albers was ‘‘unani-
mously elected Professor of Art for the period ending June 12, 1934."'?°

Albers was soon approached by more prestigious institutions; and on
March 13, fearful that he would leave, the faculty ‘‘unanimously”’
granted him ‘‘permanent tenure." Philip Johnson and Alfred Barr were
eager to have him closer to New York, and initially Albers would have
liked to have been closer to a metropolitan center, where he could have
continued the sandblasted glass paintings on which he had been work-
ing in Germany. In the spring of 1934, he was interviewed by Robert
Leigh, president of Bennington College; and in 1937 Constance Warren,
president of Sarah Lawrence College, approached him about replacing
René d'Harnoncourt in the art department. It was from Harvard Univer-
sity, however, that the most persistent offers came. Walter Gropius, who
considered Albers a ‘‘keyman"’ in his plans at Harvard, wrote to him that
he thought his ‘‘work too good for a small college.'’ He was never able,
however, to offer a permanent position, and Albers was unwilling to
resign from Black Mountain for a temporary appointment. Instead, he
gave biannual seminars at Harvard beginning in the fall of 1936 and
taught for the spring semester and first summer session in 1940. Dreier
wrote to his mother that initially Albers had thought that the whole of
the United States was like Black Mountain, but after closer association
with other colleges and universities, he came to appreciate the virtues of
Black Mountain, where there was no ecclesiastical, political, or state
control and no established tradition or faculty to contend with.?°

Albers understood the importance of new beginnings in life and in art
for breaking old habits and for revitalizing the human spirit, and his
emigration was his second ‘‘new beginning."' The first was in 1920,
when, at the age of thirty-two, after reading Gropius's flyer announcing
the opening of the Bauhaus, he abandoned his academic training to
enroll as its oldest student. Born March 19, 1888, in Bottrop, Westphalia,
Germany, into a family of craftsmen, Albers had studied first to be a
teacher. He taught primary school in the Bottrop area while continuing
his art studies at the Kunstakademie in Berlin (1913-15), at the
Kunstgewerbeschule in Essen (1916-19), and with Franz von Stuck at
                                                                                Josef Breitenbach, Josef Albers,
the Akademie in Munich (1919-20). In 1923 he was awarded his dip-

At Black Mountain Albers sought to dispel the idealization of the Euro-
pean tradition both in his teaching and in his own art. Unable to con-
tinue his sandblasted glass works because there were no facilities in the
Asheville area, he began to paint again; and there is a close correlation
between his early Bauhaus glass ‘‘paintings'’ made from broken glass
collected from the city dump and his early Black Mountain canvases. In
each case he deliberately began to work with new materials in explor-
atory, expressionistic forms that later evolved into linear, geometric pat-
terns. The primary influence on his American painting and prints was the
Pre-Columbian art of Central America, Mexico, and the Southwest,
where he and Anni Albers spent several summers and their sabbaticals.
The geometric patterns and figure-ground relationships reinforced his
interest in abstraction, in optical illusion, and in gestalt theory, which he
had studied at the Bauhaus.*”

Though isolated from major cultural centers, Albers was actively involved
in the art world; and through exhibitions of his work and, as his com-
mand of the English language improved, through his lectures, Black
Mountain came to be identified with experimental art in America. During
the 1930s, Albers had one-person exhibitions at J. B. Neumann's New
Art Circle in New York (March 9-30, 1936), at the Katharine Kuh Gallery
in Chicago (September 20-October 30, 1937), and, concurrent with the
Bauhaus exhibit at the Museum of Modern Art, at the Artists’ Gallery
(December 6-31, 1938) and the Weyhe Gallery in New York as well as in
Asheville, Havana, and Mexico City. He also exhibited with the American
Abstract Artists beginning with their first exhibition in 1937. The show
was heralded by the artists as ‘'the first large and comprehensive dem-

                                                             Despite the unsympathetic atmosphere, Albers was an aggressive advo-
                                                             cate of abstract art, especially Geometric Abstraction, which he defended
                                                             with evangelical zeal. ‘‘Abstracting,'’ he wrote, ‘‘is the essential function
                                                             of the Human Spirit. Abstract Art is the purest art: it strives most in-
                                                             tensely toward the spiritual. Abstract Art is Art in its beginning and is the
                                                             Art of the Future.'’ He saw abstract art as a natural part of an historical
                                                             development toward a ‘‘pure art,'' as part of a move away from “‘imita-
                                                             tive aims’' that pictured ‘‘nature, stories or sentiments'’ toward ‘‘non-
                                                             representative form, form that exists for its own sake, namely for form
                                                             reasons."’ Albers considered the Pre-Columbians ‘’THE representatives of
                                                             abstract Art” for their ‘truthfulness to conception and material, truthful-
                                                             ness to art as spiritual creation.'’ Through the perfect balance of formal
                                                             elements, the elimination of the trivial or extrinsic, and the absence of
                                                             mannerism, Albers sought to achieve in his compositions the spiritual
                                                             qualities he so admired in Pre-Columbian art. Furthermore, he argued,
                                                             his paintings were not sterile and without content, as his critics claimed,
                                                             but rather portrayed emotions such as sadness or wit as well as contem-
                                                             porary concepts of relativity, process, and interaction. He petitioned for
                                                             the same right as the composer to create abstract forms ‘which have
                                                             life within themselves as music has."'??

                                                             Albers had ideas about education as well as art, and as his English im-
                                                             proved, so did his impact on community life. In both his personality and
                                                             his appearance, he presented a striking contrast to John Rice. Blond,
                                                             thin, Teutonic, ascetic, and quite handsome, Albers, like Rice, was forty-
                                                             five when the college was founded. Yet unlike Rice, he was disciplined
                                                             and focused in his creative work and in his personal life. Louis Adamic
                                                             described Rice as the college's ‘‘center, its core’ and Albers as ‘‘the
                                                             strongest diffused influence on the place,"’ and Dreier noted that ‘‘Rice
                                                             is the man who makes the college a continuing possibility... but Albers
                                                             is the one who makes it turn out to be what it is more than Rice or any-
                                                             body else realizes.'’ Like Rice, Albers was often difficult to get along
                                                             with, and Dreier acknowledged that people got tired of his ‘‘attitude...
                                                             he is always so sure that he is right about everything and cannot tolerate
                                                             disagreement (except theoretically!),'' a situation all the more irritating
                                                             because Albers often turned out to be right.*°

                                                             Although not a leader in the sense that Rice and Albers were, Ted Dreier
                                                             brought to the community a tradition of independent thinking and an
                                                             adventurous and idealistic spirit which immeasurably influenced college
                                                             life. Born in 1902 in Brooklyn, New York, Dreier was the son of a promi-
                                                             nent family of idealists committed to the arts, social action, women’s
                                                             rights, and poverty programs. His grandfather, John Caspar Theodor
                                                             Dreier, left Bremen, Germany for the United States in 1849. After starting
                                                             as a clerk in the firm of Naylor and Company, he rose to the position of
                                                             senior partner and made his fortune in the iron trade. He and his wife
                                                             Dorothea instilled in their son and four daughters a profound sense of
                                                             idealism and social commitment, not to be confused with the noblesse
                                                             oblige usually associated with the wealthy. Henry Edward Dreier, Ted's
                                                             father, was a prominent businessman who was also an advocate of
                                                             women's suffrage and was active in education and social reform.
                                                             Margaret Dreier Robins and Mary were leaders in the fight for women's
                                                             suffrage and for improved conditions for the insane and were active in
                                                             the Women's Trade Union League of New York. Dorothea and Katherine
                                                             were both painters and were active in women’s suffrage and in settle-

14.   A Pioneering Venture




                                       ment houses. Katherine was a pioneering American advocate of modern
                                       art and with Marcel Duchamp and Man Ray founded the Société
                                       Anonyme, one of the finest private collections of contemporary art in
                                       the United States. Ted Dreier's mother, Ethel Eyre Dreier, was president
                                       of the Women's City Club of New York for twenty years, head of the
                                       Women's Suffrage Party of Brooklyn, and an active campaigner for
                                       Fiorello La Guardia. For all of the Dreiers, their involvement was neither
                                       dilettantish nor intellectual but represented a deep commitment to social
                                       action and an evangelical spirit. They were a family of immigrants, deter-
                                       mined to secure rights and improve hiring conditions for those less
                                       fortunate and thus repay America for what it had given them.*'

                                       Although Dreier's was a privileged and protected childhood, the pres-
                                       sures on the eldest son in so aggressive and committed a family were
                                       overwhelming. Rather than pursuing a career in social action, the arts,
                                       or business, he chose to study engineering at Harvard University. After
                                       graduation he worked for five years for the General Electric Company in
                                       Schenectady, New York. Though this position provided a necessary in-
                                       come for his young family and a stimulating and creative research atmos-
                                       phere, Dreier wished to teach. From his family he had learned respect
                                       for the power of education, and in 1930 he left General Electric to accept
                                       a teaching position at Rollins College, where his friend Malcolm Forbes
                                       was also teaching.?*

                                       Like her husband, Barbara Loines Dreier was from a family of noncon-
                                       formists, ‘‘un-regular Christians,"’ and adventurous thinkers. Her great-
                                       grandmother had gone to China on a clipper ship with an aunt and
                                       uncle and had stayed for five years. Her grandmother was a suffragist
                                       and a Unitarian, which Bobbie Dreier recalled ‘‘was as good as being a
                                       Communist in her day,'' and she married a Quaker, who was “‘read out
                                       of meeting for marrying such a radical girl.'’ Two of her aunts became
                                       Christian Scientists, and her mother left the Episcopal Church after be-

                                       Dreier's importance to the college was rooted in his allegiance to Rice
                                       and Albers, in his willingness to use his contacts and those of his family
                                       to raise money for the college, in his role as mediator and peacemaker,
                                       and in his enthusiasm, infectious idealism, and optimism. Black Mountain
                                       was a spiritual venture he entered into with the same crusading spirit
                                       that his aunts had attached to their social work. Although his thoughts
                                       were often incoherent, contradictory, and unfocused both in class and in
                                       the community, he understood the importance of financial responsibility
                                       and realized that, to a large extent, the college's credibility to the outside
                                       world would depend on its ability to balance its budget. He also recog-
                                       nized that it could not be oblivious to the opinions of others, and he
                                       wrote hundreds of letters to critics, to donors, and to friends dispelling
                                       rumors and explaining the college's goals.

                                     wealthy grandmother of one student even took the art students to the

                                     attendant charged her a dime for the items instead of the usual nickel.4®

                                     In the color class, students ‘’stud[ied] systematically the tonal possibilities
                                     of colors, their relativity, their interaction and influence on each other,
                                     cold and warmth, light intensity, color intensity, physical and spatial
                                     effects...to prepare for a disciplined use of color and to prevent acci-
                                     dent, brush, or paint-box from taking authorship.''’*? During the 1930s,
                                     Albers emphasized color-tone scales and the color systems of Goethe,
                                     Ostwald, Weber-Fechner, and others. An advanced color course concen-
                                     trated on the use of watercolors.

                                     Although Albers realized the limitations of the curriculum, which was
                                     intended for beginners, attempts to hire faculty to teach painting,
                                     sculpture, printmaking, and other areas of the visual arts were unsuccess-
                                     ful either because the artist was not interested or because the college
                                     decided the applicant was not suited to community life. Among those
                                     approached were Jean Charlot, Carlos Merida, Isamu Noguchi, Herbert
                                     Bayer, Alexander Calder, Esteban Vicente, John Graham, and Jean Arp.
                                     In letters to Wassily Kandinsky in France, Albers extolled the virtues of
                                     Black Mountain College and implored him to join the faculty. From the
                                     fall of 1936 through the spring of 1938, Alexander (Xanti) Schawinsky, a
                                     former Bauhaus student, taught the advanced students painting and
                                     drawing, and his wife Irene taught dressmaking.

                                     The basic courses were supplemented by workshops that gradually de-
                                     veloped in response to the college's need for furniture, fabrics, photo-
                                     graphs, printed items, and bookbinding. Although Albers wanted to
                                     have well-equipped workshops in weaving, woodworking, photography,
                                     printing, metalwork, sculpture, and clothing design, each headed by a
                                     ‘‘Handwerkmeister’’ as opposed to the usual ‘’arty-crafty’’ teacher, appli-
                                     cations for grants from the Carnegie Foundation in 1937 and another
                                     for $70,000 in 1941 for equipment were turned down.?° Had he been
                                     able to obtain the equipment, the program could only have been suc-
                                     cessful if the craftsmen taught on a production basis, as the college was
                                     too small to support so large a faculty in the visual arts. Albers had
                                     hoped that eventually the workshops would be self-supporting, but only
                                     the weaving workshop was able to support itself through the sale of
                                     small serviceable items such as place mats and tablecloths.

                                     The crafts workshops provided a constructive alternative to the usual
                                     courses in which students learn a little ceramics, a bit of weaving, and
                                     possibly some enameling, and which generally result in what Anni Albers
                                     aptly described as ‘‘ashtray art.’ Such courses generally foster a romantic
                                     view in which anything handmade is valued over machine-made objects
Xanti Schawinsky’s painting class,
                                     no matter how poor the craftsmanship. At Black Mountain, though,
1937. Photograph Helen M. Post.      crafts were a ‘‘means of art and manual education'’ that helped the
                                     students ‘'to learn, to see and develop discipline, taste and judgment."’
                                     Through the production of useful items for the community, the students
                                     had an opportunity to apply the principles learned in the basic courses
                                     and to learn respect for good craftsmanship.*'

                                     By far the most advanced of the workshops and the only one with a
                                     theoretical foundation was the weaving program developed by Anni
                                     Albers. Born June 12, 1899, in Berlin, Anni Fleischmann Albers had a
                                     comfortable childhood. Her mother belonged to the Ullstein publishing
                                     family, and her father was a furniture manufacturer. She was educated
                                     by tutors and later studied privately with Martin Brandenburg in Berlin
                                     and at the Kunstgewerbeschule in Hamburg. In 1922 she enrolled at the
                                     Bauhaus (Diploma, 1930), where she chose to enter the weaving work-
                                     shop; and from 1930 until her emigration in 1933, she worked as a free-
                                     lance textile designer in Dessau and Berlin. In the fall of 1931, she was a
                                     part-time instructor in the weaving workshop at the Bauhaus. On her
                                     arrival at Black Mountain, she was appointed tutor in weaving, and the
                                     following fall she was appointed to the faculty.

Anni Albers did not deny the importance of handweaving as a leisure-
time activity or its economic value as a cottage industry in rural areas,
her first commitment was to the broader social aim of designing for
industry because of the dominant role of mass production in meeting
the needs of society. She accorded the designer of industrial products a
high social and artistic responsibility because a single object reproduced
many times would enter thousands of homes. Anni Albers was disturbed,
however, by the usual situation in which a technician develops the func-
tional aspects of an object and the artist gives an outer appearance. She
defined design as ‘‘considered relationships'’ and insisted that the de-
signer as artist-craftsman be concerned with the total form and work
directly with materials rather than at a drawing board. She saw the role
of contemporary crafts as that of ‘‘restor[ing] to the designer... direct
experience of a medium”’ and was adamant in her conviction that
‘‘being creative is perhaps not so much the desire to do something but
the listening to that [which] wants to be done, the dictation of the mate-
rials."' She considered ‘'the creation of new fibres and finishes'’ through
chemistry and engineering to be the most important contemporary
contribution to the textile industry, and she often used unconventional
materials such as cellophane, aluminum, and lurex in her own designs.??

At Black Mountain Anni Albers taught weaving and textile design as ‘‘a
preparatory step to machine production,"’ which, she noted, differs from
handweaving only in ‘‘velocity'’ and the evenness of the finish. A Black
Mountain addition to her teaching technique was the practice of having
the beginning students make exploratory studies with found materials
to experience ‘‘a playful beginning, unresponsive to any demand of
usefulness, an enjoyment of colors, forms, surface contrasts and har-
monies,—a tactile sensuousness.'’ Students attempted to create the
horizontal-vertical patterns and textures of textiles while developing a
sensitivity to their surface characteristics. They then learned a vocabulary
of weaves beginning with the basic weaves—plain, twill, and satin—and
progressing to more complex variations. Through this approach, as
opposed to the usual copying of traditional patterns, she hoped to teach
the students '‘freshness of invention, of intelligent and imaginative form-
ing'' and to restore ‘‘the adventure of new exploring."

The advanced students designed textiles for specific functions, such as a
tablecloth, upholstery, a rug, or a stage curtain. For Anni Albers the
creation of a textile was not the ‘execution of a dream, as the layman
conceives it'’°* but a process involving a response to the capacities and
limitations of materials, a knowledge of the characteristics of weaves,
and an acknowledgment of the specific functional requirements for the
textile in mind. In designing a textile, the students had first to consider
its function. A wall covering, for example, should not stretch or catch
dust, must be easily attached to the wall and easily cleaned by brushing,
should have a quiet color and pattern, and should be light-reflecting and
strong. The student then chose a suitable fiber and weave, considering
production costs and such aesthetic matters as the desirability of a given
pattern, color, and texture.

Although there were similar weaving programs at the Institute of Design,
Cranbrook Academy of Art, and the Art Institute of Chicago, the Black
Mountain program produced distinctive textiles. Exhibited throughout
the United States, they were recognized for their emphasis on the thread
rather than purely coloristic or textural effects and for their limited range
of colors, primarily black, white, and natural fibers. They reflected Anni
Albers's aesthetic that textiles are serving objects that should be modest
in appearance and blend into the background.

Woodworking was added to the curriculum in response to the students’
attempts to build furniture for their studies. In the early years, Frederick
Georgia, an experienced carpenter who had built a loom for Anni Albers,
advised them on projects and furnished the chemistry lab. In the fall of
1939, Edward DuPuy, a local photographer and carpenter who owned
the Village Workshop and made the frames for Albers's paintings, came
to the college one afternoon a week to help students repair and con-
struct furniture such as bookcases and stools. DuPuy made a desk, possi-
bly designed by Albers, with a wooden surface supported on one side
by a chest of drawers and on the other by a bookcase. It was made of

Wunsch did not try to develop a professional theater at Black Mountain
but was “‘particularly interested in dramatics as an educational discipline,
as a meeting place of all the arts, as the ‘best substitute for experience,’
as a social force in a community."’ He cast students in roles entirely differ-
ent from their own personalities to help them identify with the aspira-
tions, problems, and experience of people unlike themselves. Everyone
at the college, regardless of age or talent, took part in the productions.
John Stix recalled that Wunsch's strength as a director was his ability to
take a realistic play and meticulously detail it while at the same time
avoiding a mechanical appearance. Nan Weston remembered that in

45   Art as Experience                  In his second year at the college, Schawinsky hoped to stage a contem-
                                        porary version of the dance of death. He wrote to Alfred Barr, director of
                                        the Museum of Modern Art, that the production would ‘'try to recognize
                                        the social and cultural structure of our present time, maybe under the
                                        angle of sight of ‘positive’ and ‘negative,’ and analogous to the stage
                                        representations of the Middle Ages (dance of death).'’ As a native of
                                        Basel, Schawinsky was familiar with the dance of death performed annu-
                                        ally in the streets of the city. The Black Mountain students, however, as
                                        they began studying pictorial presentations, including those of Hans
                                        Holbein, the Younger, also a citizen of Basel, decided to stage a modern
                                        dramatization rather than the philosophical parallel Schawinsky had
                                        envisioned. Typically, the experience of life and the arts at Black Moun-
                                        tain became too intimately entwined when in March Richard Porter, a
                                        student and member of the cast, committed suicide. Evarts, who was
                                        composing the music for Porter's part at the time of his death, could
                                        hardly bring himself to look at the score.®°

                                        The Danse Macabre: A Sociological Study, performed on May 14, 1938,
                                        was staged in the gymnasium in a theater-in-the-round created by three
                                        concentric circles of benches. Members of the audience, including
                                        townspeople, were cloaked in dark hoods and capes before entering to
                                        dramatize the solitude and anonymity of the individual in the face of
                                        death. At the beginning of the performance the sense of mystery was
                                        heightened by a circle of candles used for lighting due to a power failure
                                        that darkened the single overhead spotlight. Two students, Morton
                                        Steinau and Robert Sunley, had translated Dies /rae, the medieval text,
                                        and put it into poetic form. It was read to Evarts's original score and
                                        mimed by the performers, who represented twelve of the characters
                                        selected from the traditional Danse Macabre. Later Schawinsky wrote a
                                        scenario, Mondo Nova, to demonstrate what he had envisioned when
                                        the class had begun their study of the dance of death.®”

                                        In the spring of 1938 Schawinsky declined a reappointment to the
                                        faculty to accept an invitation to teach at the New Bauhaus in Chicago.
                                        He had been granted a leave of absence in May for the remainder of
                                        the semester to enter the competition with Walter Gropius, Marcel
                                        Breuer, and Herbert Bayer for the Pennsylvania pavilion at the New York
                                        World's Fair and had been awarded the design commission for the North
                                        Carolina pavilion. In the spring he traveled throughout the state with
                                        two Black Mountain students, Beverly Coleman and George
                                        Hendrickson, collecting information for the North Carolina exhibition.
                                        He returned to the college for the summer of 1938, and when Laszlo
                                        Moholy-Nagy canceled the appointments of younger instructors to the
                                        New Bauhaus, Schawinsky asked Black Mountain to reconsider his
                                        reappointment.®®

                                        The faculty denied his request. Warm, temperamental, enthusiastic,
                                        devious, and fun-loving, Schawinsky was Black Mountain's ‘‘bull in a
                                        china shop." He was more likely to throw an ashtray to get the desired

than Hawthorne, Whitman, or Stein. American literature was taught
primarily by Wunsch and as a part of courses in literary forms, such as
Mangold's course in problems of the novel, which included Gertrude
Stein's The Making of Americans. Some of the most popular courses
were Mangold's courses in Stendhal, Flaubert, and Proust. Kurtz taught
semester-long explications of Fyodor Dostoyevsky's Crime and Punish-
ment and Thomas Mann's Magic Mountain. In many respects the teach-
ing of literature was approached in much the same way as the teaching
of music. Emphasis was placed on oral readings of fiction, poetry, and
drama, which were studied within the broader context of the historical
and cultural life of their time. Joe Martin recalled that as a teacher he
was not so much concerned with what happened between the student
and the teacher as with what happened between the student and
the literature.?°

Creative writing was taught during the 1930s by John Rice, although
Robert Wunsch, William McCleery, and Fred Mangold also taught at
times. Rice's writing seminar, attended by both faculty and students, met
after dinner at eight and often did not break up until after midnight.
Louis Adamic noted that ‘‘Things happened in that class."'?' The partici-
pants read their essays, poems, radio scripts, newspaper articles, and
other creative works which were then discussed by the whole class. The
1939-40 catalogue stated that ‘‘writing is one of the severest of disci-
plines, and that even the most modest mastery of it is an enriching
achievement.'' The focus was on writing as an ‘‘artistic and creative
medium,’’ with an emphasis on ‘‘art expression as distinguished from
self-expression."’ Acute observation and the most effective use of the
language in recording that observation or insight were valued over
formal innovation per se.

The students could usually count on visiting writers to critique their
work. When Gerald Heard and Aldous Huxley visited in May 1937, there
were discussions at general community meetings, picnics, and individual
critiques. Heard, who had recently published an article on psychic re-
search, led a general discussion on the capacities of the mind through
mental telepathy and clairvoyance. Charles Norman, a friend of William
McCleery, visited for ten days to give a lecture on Christopher Marlowe.
He also gave a reading of his own poems and at the students’ request
read the poems of E. E. Cummings as well. When John Preston visited in
March 1936, Mangold wrote that before a reading of the work of
Gertrude Stein, Surette was “'‘primed to take both Stein and Preston for
a ride” but ‘‘got about half converted during his reading."' In the fall of
1940, May Sarton stopped at the college for ten days to lecture, give
readings, discuss the college's educational program, and give individual
writing critiques. Not long after she left, Henry Miller and Abraham
Rattner ‘‘dropped in one evening" unannounced. John Evarts recalled
that fortunately a few of the ‘‘avant-gardists'’ had read Miller's The

 interesting, beautifully, softly burning, blue-flamed hickory logs.''?”

 The college was primarily supported by tuition and small gifts, especially
 from individuals in the Northeast, where there was a tradition of experi-
 mental education. The tuition and fees of $1,000 were high for the time;
 however, students were charged on a sliding scale according to their
 ability to pay. The average reduction of thirty percent had to be made
 up in gifts. There was no endowment, and the faculty was unwilling to
 accept gifts if they carried with them an effort to influence the college's
 program. To reassure its supporters, the college selected William Morse
 Cole, Professor of Accounting, Emeritus, of Harvard University, as
 auditor. Cole visited the college twice yearly and, besides performing the
 audit, conducted readings in Shakespeare. During the first year, the
 faculty drew only $960.15 in expenses, an average of $7.27 per month
 per faculty member, in addition to the $1,000 gift for the Alberses. The
 year ended with expenditures of $24,181.30 and a balance of $1,591.97,
 plus the $5,300 of the underwriting that had been called for the first
 year but had not been used.”® So surprised were the underwriters that,
 with the exception of Margaret Lewisohn, they gave that portion to the
 college as a gift. Although the students and faculty liked to surmise
 what they might have done if offered a million dollars with no strings          Thornton Wilder, February 1934.
 attached, it was not a problem they ever had to face.                           Photograph courtesy North Carolina
                                                                                 State Archives (Black Mountain
                                                                                 College Papers).
  Despite a successful campaign to place articles in newspapers and
  magazines, raising money was extremely difficult. Those who praised
  the college's idealism were generally unwilling to put their money behind
  it. Foundations made small grants for immediate operating expenses, for
  the salary of a particular faculty member (this was especially the case
_ with the refugee faculty), or to pay a student's tuition; however, without
_ trustees to assure continuity of purpose or longevity, they were unwilling
_ to make grants for long-term projects. The William C. Whitney Founda-
  tion, the only foundation to consistently support the college, gave grants
  of $1,000 to $3,000 annually from 1933 through 1948. The Marshall
  Field Foundation eventually responded to the college's pleas for money
  with a pedigreed bull for the farm and with a small grant. On holidays,
  students and faculty would sponsor teas, concerts, and lectures and pass
  the hat. Ted Dreier and John Evarts, both of whom had connections with
 prominent individuals in the New York and Boston areas, used their influ-
 ence to raise money.”” The largest single contributions came from
 Malcolm Forbes, who provided the bulk of the underwriting for the
 college's founding, and from Stephen Forbes, the son of Malcolm Forbes's
 half-sister, who provided funds to help the college pay salaries for
 the faculty.

Asheville in his behalf and for Mangold himself to “pick out...a tie of
the appropriate colour" and ‘‘take along [his] Lion's Club badge." After
a brief solicitous period before the townspeople realized that the college
was not going to be a boon to the economy, the relationship settled into
one of mutual tolerance. At the same time, there were those among the
local residents for whom the concerts, drama productions, lectures, and
other events were a welcome addition to community life. From 1938
through 1944, the college sponsored a weekly series of radio programs
of concerts, lectures, play readings, panel discussions, and other activities
on WWNC in Asheville. An employee of the station wrote to the college
that ‘‘we want you to know we really appreciate your efforts to keep a
‘listening’ audience, which is not easy.'"'°°

Within the state of North Carolina and the Southeast, Black Mountain
identified with the liberal leadership that gave the college its support.
Frank Graham, president of the University of North Carolina, and Francis
Bradshaw, dean at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, were
instrumental in obtaining approval for the college for benefits under the
Gl Bill of Rights after the war, and, with some effort, convinced the
administration of the university to accept Black Mountain credits for
transfer and its graduates for advanced study. Other leaders in the arts,
such as John Allcott, head of the department of art at Chapel Hill, en-
couraged their students to visit the college and arranged exhibitions of
the work of Black Mountain faculty and students. Rice noted that several
North Carolina educators had told him “‘in private that they were de-
lighted to have a frankly experimental college in the state.""'°”

Black Mountain College was apolitical, and when stands were taken on
political issues, as they often were, they were taken by individuals. Its
reputation as a Communist community was based solely on its experi-
mental nature and unconventional life-style. Ironically, there was often
as much Red-baiting going on within the college as outside. Albers, who
had himself experienced the oppression of political ideology when
Hannes Meyer, a Communist, was director of the Bauhaus, feared the
development of a cell within the community and was constantly on the
lookout for a potential Communist. John Rice got into trouble over a
lecture he gave for the PTA in Charlotte, North Carolina. He said that
‘parenthood is a very painful and unhappy condition...children are
general nuisances" and that ‘‘the earth is not the center of the universe”
and humans not the ‘special darlings of the God that created
them...but only one point in a long line of evolution.'’ He further de-
clared man not to be solely a creature of reason but closer to the ape
than he might like to think. The address resulted in an “impromptu
indignation meeting” after the lecture and a host of articles in the local
papers reporting accusations that Rice and the college were ‘‘decidedly
radical and communistic.'' When Rice stated, ‘| do not approve of the
totalitarian state," it was said that he ‘‘slurred at democracy.'""%

A chronic problem and one that consumed a tremendous amount of
time was the rental of the Blue Ridge property. Less than a month after
the college opened, foreclosure proceedings were initiated by bond-
holders against the owner, the Blue Ridge Association; and the property
was sold at auction on October 2, 1933, an action which negated the
college's lease.'°? Although the fledgling college wanted to purchase
the property, it could not raise the funds to do so. Eventually, Willis
Weatherford, president of the YMCA Graduate School in Nashville and
executive secretary of the Blue Ridge Association, managed to regain
the property in the name of Blue Ridge College, Inc. Thereafter
Weatherford was as tenacious in his determination to hold on to the
land as the college was to negotiate the best possible lease, and each
year the ‘‘Weatherford Watchers’ sought to assess the proximity of the

  After a leave of absence at Folly Beach in South Carolina in the spring of
  1938 and another for the academic year 1939-40 in Southern Pines,
  North Carolina, Rice offered his resignation at the faculty's request.
  Wunsch and Nell Rice, who was studying library science at Chapel Hill,
  made several trips to Southern Pines to try to resolve the situation. Nell
  refused a reconciliation and planned to return to the college as librarian.
  Rice did not feel he should return unless she was willing to take him
  back. He had made and broken so many promises to both his wife and
  the college that neither had confidence that upon his return he would
  be any different. In a note to Wunsch, Rice reassured him, ‘‘In the long
  reach of time this thing that now seems earth-shaking will not so much
  as stir a blade of grass, only a little laughter, at least over the second
  old-fashioned. Please do not think that it has lessened my affection for
  you; rather, that it has deepened.''""”

on a two-bedroom house for Johanna and Heinrich Jalowetz. Kocher's             Harvey Campbell.
design, based on four-by-eight-foot plywood units, used transite facing,
plywood, steel sash windows, and insulation. The living room, which
also served as a music classroom, had space for a grand piano, special
shelving for Jalowetz's collection of sheet music, and bookcases for his
library. The plywood panels at the end of the living room where the
piano was to be located were perforated to improve the acoustics, and
sound-deadening vermiculite plaster was used in the ceiling. Within the
next eighteen months, a two-and-a-half-story barn and two tile silos
were built. The use of unskilled labor provided its humorous moments.
At one point cup grease was mistaken for asphalt cement and used to
attach the roofing to the Jalowetz house. The mistake was discovered
when Roscoe Penley, the farmer, needed the cup grease. At another
time, Molly Gregory and a student tried to route a sewer uphill.°

As each stone was laid and each window purchased, the faculty and
students worked frantically to raise money to pay the bills. The college's
financial reserves had been exhausted by the purchase of the Lake Eden
property, and the 1940 summer fund-raising campaign had been unsuc-
cessful. Construction was started with $2,900 on hand: $2,200 was
allocated from the general budget and $700 from the summer gifts. The
faculty sacrificed sixty percent of their salaries (they had taken cuts the
previous two years). Molly Gregory recalled that when she arrived in
1941, there were so few tools that the students ‘‘practically used their
front teeth," a situation she found typical of educational institutions,
where “‘labor's cheap."' As construction progressed and the college man-
aged to get good publicity, fund raising was easier. Armed with a picture
bulletin, ‘‘What Your Dollar Will Buy,"’ the students raised $6,300 over
the Christmas vacation by organizing teas, lectures, musicales, and other
events. It was an impressive sum, especially since most of the money
came from very small gifts. As Fred Mangold noted: ‘‘Mendez [Marks]
has culled $4.33 from some relations who gave him some old silver to
sell that they had contemplated giving to Aid to Great Britain. In Boston
Mme [Germaine] Monteux gave an informal concert at which they
passed the hat and got $55. Another $7.50 has also come in from the
Mass. outfit. The kids sound excited and busy and it's all very cheering."’
Articles appeared in newspapers and magazines throughout the country,
including a full page of color photographs by John Stix in the St. Louis
Post-Dispatch Uanuary 12, 1941). A fund-raising trip by John Evarts to
California in the summer of 1941 netted copies of Between Two Worlds
and World's End from Upton Sinclair, enough small cash contributions
from Melvyn Douglas and others to almost cover his expenses, and an
effort, though unsuccessful, by Henry Fonda to get Evarts onto the
‘We, the People’’ show. The actual cost of the studies building was about
$48,000, and the faculty estimated the value of student and faculty
 labor at about $25,000.’

    The move from the stately buildings of Blue Ridge to the rough terrain
    of Lake Eden brought tragedy to the small community. In August 1940
    Morton Steinau, the assistant treasurer, and Frank Nacke, a student,
    went out in a boat in a heavy rain to open the gates to the Lake Eden
    dam. They were washed over, and Nacke's body was found the next
    morning, left behind by the receding waters. A year later, Mark Dreier,
    the nine-year-old son of Bobbie and Ted Dreier, died instantly when the
    college truck overturned, tossing him from the running board on which
    he was riding.

i   In 1942 Alex Reed, a former student who had returned to teach art
    during Albers's 1940-41 sabbatical, designed and constructed a small
    stone Quiet House in memory of Mark. Often described as a Quaker
    meetinghouse, it was a place of meditation, a temporary escape from
    the tensions of community life, and a setting for special occasions such
    as weddings and funerals. Reed gathered the stone from the campus,
    built wooden benches with the assistance of Molly Gregory, and wove
    the curtains himself. Mark's ashes were buried at the base of a giant tree
    in front of the Quiet House and those of Frank Nacke in a rhododendron
    grove where Heinrich Jalowetz and Max Dehn were also later buried.®

    The war forced the termination of construction, and in April 1943 Kocher
    was given a leave of absence to complete an article he was writing with
    Howard Dearstyne, who had briefly taught at the college. They en-
    visioned a postwar comprehensive architectural center that would coordi-
    nate research, industry, private practice of architects and engineers,
    architectural and technical schools, town and city planning, the social
    and psychological aspects of architecture, and public education.” Kocher
    visited briefly in the summer of 1943, but though the leave was ex-
    tended until after the war, he decided not to return. In 1928 he had
    been appointed to the Advisory Committee of Architects for the Restora-
    tion of Colonial Williamsburg in Virginia, and after leaving Black Moun-
    tain, he was appointed editor of the Architectural Records for Colonial
    Williamsburg and lecturer in fine arts and architecture at The College of
    William and Mary. For the remainder of the war years, Horace McGuire
    (Mac) Wood, a contractor and designer of small houses who was director
    of the college work program, taught basic courses in architecture.

     As the end of the war approached, the college hoped to revive the
     architecture program. In May 1945, on Gropius's recommendation, Paul
     Beidler, an architect who had studied with Frank Lloyd Wright at Taliesin,
     was appointed to teach architecture. An experienced architect who was
     interested in education and community, he seemed to be just the person
     the college had been seeking. In the spring and summer of 1945, he
     designed and constructed a charming music practice room of glass,
     concrete, and wood which blended beautifully with the surrounding
     pine grove. The trapezoidal shape with slanting glass walls on two sides
     was chosen to improve the acoustics and give a sense of spaciousness to
     the small room. Beidler noted that the construction of the music practice
     room with student help offered ‘‘a nostalgic glimpse of the satisfactions
     which lay in the old master-builder apprentice relationship,'’ in contrast
     to the modern situation in which the ‘‘architect and his product are...at
     Opposite ends of the assembly line.'’'° The room was inaugurated on
     July 9, 1945, with the singing of Handel's Largo by Carol Brice and a
     short address by Albers. Unfortunately for the college, at the end of the

                                     The most serious challenge to the college's educational ideas during the
                                     war years came through Eric Bentley, a young Englishman who had
                                     taught for a year at UCLA after receiving his doctorate from Yale. At
                                     UCLA he had run into difficulties with the administration, and Galka
                                     Scheyer, whom he met at a party, suggested that he apply to Black
                                     Mountain. Bentley, who was twenty-five years old at the time wrote to
                                     the college that he was attracted by the ideal of ‘‘work, culture, and
                                     community.’ After teaching as guest faculty for the summer of 1942, he
                                     moved to New York, where he married a Black Mountain student, Maya
                                     Tschernjakow, and considered joining the Canadian services. Bentley
                                     had serious reservations about the compatibility of his ideas about edu-
                                     cation and those of the college. His description of the ideal teacher in
                                     the humanities as ‘‘a humane person, learned & alive, absorbed &
                                     delighted with his subject....a surgeon at the operating table, & the
                                     students stand looking over his shoulder— watching his work" conflicted
                                     with Rice's ideal of the teacher on one end of the log and the student on
                                     the other. He begrudgingly acknowledged the necessity of the work
                                     program yet was critical of ‘‘the religious cult of Work"' or of any attempt
                                     to justify the work program pedagogically.°

                                     There were those at the college who were not without reservations of
                                     their own. Dreier wrote to Bentley that a major criticism was that he
                                     ‘would enjoy building up a loud-mouthed clique who were really less
                                     socially aware and thoughtful than others,'’ and he was thus ‘‘likely to
                                     be a destructive rather than constructive force in the community."'
                                     Bentley's contempt for the English system of government and his admira-
                                     tion for the Soviet system led to accusations of Stalinism and Com-
                                     munism, and some felt that he was more interested in ‘‘propaganda”’
                                     than in teaching. Bentley denied being a Communist, although he al-
                                     lowed that he would readily take a Communist on the faculty if he were
                                     “learned & stimulating."’ He wrote further, ‘‘My own predilections are
                                     towards American pragmatism, belief in the common         man, economic
                                     democracy, social democracy. ...The method of my thought is positivistic,
                                     materialistic, if you will, but only because | believe that non-materialistic
                                     philosophies are hostile to that very ‘spirit of man’ which they praise.''*'

had not tried to make a point of it to the local community because “we
have always thought it wise not to wave a red flag in front of a bull.'’ As
 discussions continued, the sides became more sharply polarized. Finally,
on April 24, a compromise was reached: “It is agreed that in principle
 the college is in favor of taking Negro members in the Summer Institutes,
 but that for practical reasons the number should be limited to one qual-
 ified female member" (it was suggested by Charlotte Hawkins Brown
that two should be admitted, since the one might otherwise be lonely).
A spring seminar on ‘‘the texture and mind of the South" to educate
community members was also planned. Thus the spring 1944 quarter
ended with the issue settled temporarily and with peace restored.7®

 Unfortunately, the long-awaited peace lasted only a few weeks. In July
 two students, Jeanne Wacker and Barbara Anderson Dupee, both of
 whom were part of the Bentley-Foreman group, decided to hitchhike to
Nashville, Tennessee, to visit Bentley, who was teaching at Fisk University
 in June and July. On the return trip, they were arrested in Chattanooga
 and charged with loitering (that is, prostitution). The girls were given
 sixty-day jail sentences and blood tests, and it was reported incorrectly
 that one of the girls had venereal disease. Neither Bentley nor Foreman,
 who was working during the summer with the CIO Political Action Com-
                                                                                Charles Beard visits the college.

The crisis threatenend to disrupt the summer sessions in the arts. Sam          Photograph John Harvey Campbell.
 Brown, the student moderator who was attending the Music Insitute,
 recalled that he found himself ‘‘living between heaven and hell simul-
taneously,''*? with many of the guest faculty and students only vaguely
aware of the bitter recriminations taking place behind closed doors. The
issue would not rest, as the girls were being made into heroes by many
 of the students, and the faculty felt a need to settle the controversy
 before the fall term opened.

A majority of the faculty expressed their lack of confidence in de Graaff,
the students’ advisor, for not having discouraged them from hitchhiking
_and requested the Board take action. Although some had earlier com-
plained that they felt de Graaff was too lenient, the real source of dis-
‘comfort was her devotion to Bentley. Undoubtedly, she was, to a certain
|extent, made a scapegoat for the tensions of the previous year. The
Board considered and tabled a resolution requesting that both de Graaff
and Bentley decline the renewal of their appointments for the next year,
“since it is not possible to build two different kinds of colleges in the
 same place at the same time." To protest, Clark Foreman, Fritz Cohen,
 and Elsa Kahl, as well as a large group of students, resigned. In his letter
 of resignation, Bentley charged that the college was a ‘‘dictatorship,”’
 not a ‘liberal institution,"’ and that it was dominated by ‘‘many
 moralists, mediocrities, and reactionaries.'’ Heinrich Jalowetz, who felt
 sympathy with both sides, asked for a leave until the end of the Summer
 Music Institute and for temporary leaves should other professional op-
 portunities present themselves in the future. He recognized that the split
 represented an ‘‘amputation in which the body of the College will lose
 more young blood than can be good for its healthy survival.'"°°

                                        Also appointed to teach writing in the fall of 1944 was George Zabriskie, _
                                        a recent graduate of Duke University. Zabriskie had heard about Black
                                        Mountain through his wife, who had known Molly Gregory at
                                        Bennington, and through Katharine Gilbert, head of the Fine Arts
                                        Department at Duke. Despite his youth, he had already published his
                                        first book of poems The Mind's Geography (1941) and had received a
                                        Guggenheim fellowship. His course Patterns in Psychology and
                                        Aesthetics (Psychodynamics of Creativity) explored the nature of the
                                        creative personality and its interaction with society. Zabriskie himself
                                        epitomized the romantic image of the poet. The Zabriskies shared a
                                        cottage with the Lowinskys, and Gretel Lowinsky recalled that Zabriskie's
                                        wife warned her that he would become ill at the sight or smell of warm
                                        milk. One day, by mistake, a cup of coffee she was serving in his pres-
                                        ence had a skim of cream on the top, and he fell into a faint in his wife's
                                        arms. A lover of trains, Zabriskie had model trains running all over the
                                        apartment. Investigating a strange noise one day, Gretel Lowinsky
                                        discovered that he was sawing a hole in the bathroom door through
                                        which the train could pass.*” He met Lyonel Feininger at the college in
                                        1944, and their shared fascination with trains led to a lifelong exchange
                                        of poems, letters, and prints.
