‘175   The European Tradition at Black Mountain   From 1940 to 1942 music was taught by Heinrich Jalowetz, John Evarts,
                                                  Jessie Ann Nelson Engle, Trudi Straus, and Johanna Jalowetz. Engle, a
                                                  young American musician and recent graduate of Bennington College,
                                                  had been recommended to the college by Ruth Ives, another Bennington
                                                  graduate who at the time was teaching at Converse College in South
                                                  Carolina. For her first year, she was an apprentice teacher, and in the
                                                  second year she was appointed to the faculty. She resigned after the
                                                  death of her fiancé Richard Carpenter in the summer of 1942.
                                                  In the fall of 1942, Evarts was given an indeterminate leave of absence
                                                  with the expectation that he would return after the war.?® Jalowetz
                                                  was then joined by two young European musicians, Fritz Cohen and
                                                  Edward Lowinsky.

                                                  Cohen, a composer, pianist, and conductor, was thirty-eight years old
                                                  when he arrived at Black Mountain. Educated at the Conservatory and
                                                  University of Leipzig, he had been director for drama and opera at the
                                                  Theater der Stadt Minster, where he met Kurt Jooss, and at the Stadt-
                                                  theater in Wurzburg. In Essen he was stage director and conductor for
                                                  the Municipal Opera House and conductor, composer, and pianist for
                                                  the Folkwang Tanztheater Studio (Neue Tanzbiihne). With Jooss he had
                                                  been instrumental in founding the Ballets Jooss, and he composed many
                                                  of its dance scores, including that for the The Green Table, a contempo-
                                                  rary dance of death and a bitter statement against the glorification of
                                                  war. The dance won first prize in 1932 at the International Congress of
                                                  the Dance sponsored by Les Archives Internationales de la Danse in
                                                  Paris, which brought international acclaim to the fledging dance troupe.
                                                  The Nazis, however, were offended by the anti-war sentiment of the
                                                  dance as well as by its experimental form, and this along with the exis-
                                                  tence of both Jews and homosexuals in the troupe made it dangerous
                                                  for the dancers to remain in Germany after the appointment of Hitler in
                                                  1933. In 1934 Dorothy Whitney Elmhirst offered the dancers a refuge at
                                                  Dartington Hall in Devon, England. Using this as a home base from
                                                  1934 until 1940, they made international tours in the fall and spring. At
                                                  the end of the American tour in April 1940, a return was not possible for
                                                  those who held German passports, and the troupe was rescued by impre-
                                                  sario Leon Greanin, who arranged a fifteen-month South American tour.

                                                  After their return to the United States in June 1941, Cohen composed
                                                  the music for Drums Sound in Hackensack, a dance comedy written and
                                                  choreographed by Agnes de Mille and premiered by the Ballets Jooss at
                                                  the Maxine Elliott Theatre in New York. The play had only a short run,
                                                  and after it closed, the troupe disbanded. Cohen and his wife Elsa Kahl
                                                  found themselves with no means of support. The William C. Whitney
                                                  Foundation, which had been a supporter of both the ballet and Black
                                                  Mountain, provided a fellowship for Cohen and for his wife to join the
                                                  college's faculty.

                                                  Also appointed in the fall of 1942 was Edward Lowinsky, a young pianist
                                                  and musicologist who was to play a critical role in the establishment of
                                                  scholarly standards and methodology in the emerging field of American
                                                  musicology, especially in the study of early music. His salary for the first
                                                  two years was provided by the Emergency Committee in Aid of Dis-
                                                  placed Foreign Scholars. Lowinsky was born in Stuttgart in 1908 to
                                                  Russian-Jewish parents and held a Nansen passport issued by the League
                                                  of Nations. He studied at the University of Heidelberg with Karl Jaspers
                                                  in philosophy and Heinrich Besseler in musicology. In 1933 he fled to
                                                  Holland, where he lectured for music societies and taught music pri-
                                                  vately. From there he escaped with his wife Gretel to Cuba and then
                                                  gained entry to the United States, where he taught in New York and
                                                  traveled throughout the country to study music teaching methods.

                                                  The effect of the appointment of the European faculty to the music
                                                  department was a higher degree of professionalism, a broader range of
                                                  courses, and a richer musical life in general. Surette’s collection of books,
                                                  recordings, and scores was the foundation for a music library. In addition,
                                                  Fritz Hansgirg had a Steinway grand piano and a Hammond organ,
                                                  which he let the college use, as well as a valuable collection of recordings
                                                  of European operas. There was a community chorus, and a cappella
                                                  chorus, a vocal ensemble, an instrumental ensemble, and the collegium

In the spring the faculty considered appointing Fernand Léger, who had
written to Lawrence Kocher to inquire about a teaching position. During
a February visit, Léger lectured on the relationship of painting to archi-
tecture, gave a demonstration of the Ballet mechanique, and held class-
room discussions and individual conferences with students. Kenneth
Kurtz recalled that the public lecture was in French with Lucian Marquis,
who had lived in several different countries on his route from Germany,
translating into English, Spanish, and German. Léger also made an
impression out of the classroom. When the women students went for
their pre-dinner showers after working in construction, Léger would join

same respect as the other studies. To demonstrate that quartiers de nob-
lesse do not exist among objects, Anni Albers and Alex Reed designed
‘hardware jewelry,’’ which was exhibited throughout the United States.

In all studies Albers was interested in the ratio of effort to effect; and his
students’ notes are sprinkled with adages such as ''Great design is sim-
ple. Save your energy, save your scissors'’ and ‘'Simplicity means reduc-
tion of complexity. To be simple today is a social obligation.'' Ruth Asawa
recalled that after meticulously shading paper with a pencil to create the
appearance of a full page of a newspaper, Albers pointed out to her that
she might have completed the exercise in half the time had she ‘‘folded”
the page. In a subsequent exercise in which she pricked a piece of blotter
paper to give the impression of a terry cloth washcloth, she dutifully
folded a corner to show that the lesson was well taken. In addition to
the studies in construction and combination, there were studies in pro-
portion, optical illusion, and figure-ground relationships.*”

Through the color course, published as Interaction of Color (1963),
Albers made a major contribution to our understanding of color percep-
tion by exploring the interaction of colors as we perceive them. Only
paper was used for the studies because of the changes in color that
paint undergoes as it dries and the difficulty of duplicating exactly a
previously mixed color. Albers had a collection of colored papers that he
got from manufacturers, and he kept it in a huge suit box. At the begin-
ning of class, he put the box in the middle of the room and students
scrounged for desired colors. Unused scraps were carefully returned to
the collection at the end of class.*® Although with papers it was not
possible to mix colors, Albers designed exercises in which the students
tried to find a piece of paper the color that would be produced if two
transparent sheets of different colors were overlapping one another.
There were also exercises to demonstrate the change in a single color
when placed on two different colors and, more difficult, the problem of          Ruth Asawa, Exercise in color place-

Although he continued to use curvilinear lines in his prints during the           Foundation.
early 1940s, Albers's work became increasingly geometric during the war
years. At Harvard in the spring of 1941, he created his Graphic Tectonics
drawings, which were later printed as zinc lithographs in Hickory, North
Carolina. His abstract art remained as controversial in the college com-
munity as it was in the public sphere. Marilyn Bauer Greenwald recalled
that when she arrived, students were circulating the story that he had
once made a painting using two different colors on differently shaped
areas that were supposed to cover exactly the same amount of space.
As the story was told, to ensure that the areas were equal, he had cut
the shapes out of paper and carried them to the science lab, where he
weighed them on the scales."

The most important addition to the visual arts program during the war
years was the architecture curriculum. In the summer of 1940, Kocher
wrote to Dreier that he would be ‘‘interested in conducting some student
instruction in design partly related to what may be termed ‘shelter and
furnishings.’ '' He noted that his course would be “‘in the nature of train-
ing in thinking with respect to forms and requirements of the setting for
living and work." As a designer Kocher was primarily interested in the
social responsibility of the architect rather than in the creation of master-
pieces for wealthy individuals. He felt that ‘‘design should relate to reality;
the reality of the life for today; the houses for improved living; improved
community planning; and a richer life which presupposes the philosophy
of surroundings that are attractive, sanitary and efficient." In an article
on the small house written at the college, Kocher advocated the building
of low-cost housing that would use lightweight, prefabricated, mass-
produced parts; would be visually appealing and comfortable; and
would be intimately related to the landscape. He sought ‘‘the maximum
utilization of space while retaining the appearance of spaciousness,"’
and he recognized the importance of designing furniture and storage
space to accommodate the estimated ‘'10,000 articles that ordinarily
clutter up the house." As part of the architecture curriculum, he taught
a course in furniture design and designed several pieces of furniture
himself. He was convinced that the potential in prefabrication for visual
monotony could be overcome by carefully placing the houses, by avoid-
ing the box motif, and by varying the design of the components.
Kocher's zeal for small-house design was given new impetus when he
observed the one-room shacks in which many of the local mountain
people lived.??

The pre-architecture curriculum was unique in its combination of basic
courses taught by Albers, experience in workshops in the crafts, classes
in modern architectural design and materials as well as in furniture de-
sign, and practical construction experience. Unlike the construction
requirement at most architecture schools, where students were assigned
to work on a particular site, the Black Mountain plan involved them in
the design, planning, and fund raising in addition to the actual building.
The program was also exceptional in that the training took place within
the context of the general liberal arts curriculum. Charles Burchard, a
Harvard graduate who later taught architecture for a summer session,
noted that the architecture curriculum at Black Mountain in the 1940s
was what Carpenter Center at Harvard University later became and
what Gropius wanted to have at the time but was stopped by bureau-
cratic and academic impositions.?? Gropius encouraged his Harvard
students to study at Black Mountain with Albers and to take part in the
construction program to fulfill their Harvard construction requirement.
Black Mountain students were also well prepared for advanced architec-
ture study. Several of Kocher's students—   Don Page, Charles Forberg,
Alex Reed, Claude Stoller, and Robert Bliss— attended Harvard and MIT
for graduate work in architecture and pursued distinguished careers as
teachers, designers, and architects.

Kocher was assisted at different times by four young architects: Willo
von Moltke, Howard Dearstyne, Anatole Kopp, and Lou Bernard Voigt.
Von Moltke, who taught as an apprentice teacher from November 13,
1940, until Christmas, was a German-born immigrant who had received
his diploma in architecture from the Technische Hochschule in Berlin
before coming to the United States. While working for Alvar Aalto and
Oskar Stonorov, he met Xanti Schawinsky, who recommended Black
Mountain to him. The following year Howard Dearstyne was appointed
to teach from November 1941 through May 1942. The only American-
born student to graduate from the Bauhaus, Dearstyne had worked for
Wallace K. Harrison and J. A. Fouilhoux in New York and for Raymond
Lowey, Antonin Raymond, and others after his return to the United
States. Anatole Kopp, a Parisian of Russian parentage, had studied at
the University of Paris and at the Ecole spéciale d'architecture, before his
escape to the United States. He had attended MIT, where he had com-
pleted his course requirements for his master's degree when John
Burchard recommended him to the college. He and his wife attended
the 1942 summer work camp for a week, and in November 1942 he

On September 12 the entire music faculty sent Schoenberg a telegram,
“in devotion to the creator,"’ announcing the concerts and lectures.°”

Albers was able to attract an equally eminent group of European and
young American artists for the Art Institute, which opened two weeks
after the Music Institute and closed September 16. To accommodate the
needs of the many teachers enrolled, he chose as his theme ‘‘the teach-
ing of art.'’ Unlike most art education seminars, which taught methodol-
ogy and artsy-craftsy classroom projects, the Black Mountain program
sought to bring together teachers and practicing, creative artists. Just as
the Music Institute valued interpretation over virtuosity, the Art Institute
emphasized ‘‘effective observation, and more intuitive perception’’ over
“technical information as well as a so-called art appreciation.''©®

Although in later years most of the summer faculty were hired for the
entire summer, in the summer of 1944 only the French-born artist Jean
Charlot was at the college all summer. He had been assistant to the
Mexican muralist Diego Rivera and between 1926 and 1929 had taken
part in the archaeological expeditions in the Yucatan, including Chichén
Itza. In the summer of 1944, Charlot, whom Albers had tried to attract
to the faculty since 1939, was in transit between teaching positions at
the University of Georgia in Athens and Smith College. In addition to his
courses in drawing, painting from nature, and composition, he gave a
series of community lectures on ‘‘Masters and Their Epochs'' and painted
two frescoes Learning and Inspiration, on the pylons beneath the studies
building. Along with the open rehearsals of the string quartet, the paint-
ing of the frescoes was a focus of community life for the summer. While
at the college, Charlot also wrote the synopsis for his book The Mexican
Mural Renaissance, 1920-25 (1963).

Direct carving in stone was taught by José de Creeft, who was at the
college from August 7 until the end of the session. As a young sculptor
in France, de Creeft had abandoned the academic tradition of first mod-
eling a figure in plaster in favor of direct carving in stone. Confronted
with a complete lack of sculpting tools at Black Mountain, he built a
forge and taught the students to make their own tools. As the bitter
conflict culminating in the resignations of Cohen, Kahl, Bentley, and
others raged, de Creeft staged a colorful bullfight burlesque, in which
he played the matador, to provide a little comic relief. The dining hall
was quickly transformed into an arena for the spectacle, in which ‘‘there
was a matador; there were toreadors, picador-mounted horses, ferocious
bulls, Spanish ladies with long eyebrows and eyelashes and with flowers
in their hair, a Spanish president, cigarette girls, arena shovelers, and a
civil guard."’ In keeping with the carnival atmosphere, ‘‘the admission
price to the spectators gallery was a cigarette and a nickel.'"©? De Creeft
further astounded the college in the fall when he married Lore Goulet,
one of the college's art students, who happened to be less than a
third his age.

Walter Gropius, whose daughter Ati was a student at the college, deliv-
ered two lectures on ‘‘Site and Shelter after the War,'’ and Amédée
Ozenfant, the founder of the Purist movement in France, gave lectures
over a two-week period on ‘'Why Mankind Really Needs Art"’ and ‘‘Art
and Philosophy: the Preforms."’ Albers had met Ozenfant when the
latter visited the Bauhaus, and his Purist painting had exerted an influ-
ence on Albers's work. At Black Mountain, Ozenfant made a series of
drawings of the mountain christened '‘Mae West'' by the college and of
its silhouette reflected in Lake Eden. Later in New York he painted at
least three interpretations of the motif in different colors representing
the seasons. Ozenfant, who described the college as ‘‘a petite university,
isolated in nature like a Benedictine abbey,"' found it odd to be a French-
man in what he described as ‘‘one of the new centers of German cul-
ture’’ in America. At the same time he wrote that though aware ‘‘that
there are still German soldiers in my home," he felt he and his German
colleagues were ‘‘servants of the same creed: that of the Sorbonne, of
Heidelberg, of Oxford, of Salamanque."'”°

One of the most popular courses was the clothing course taught by
Bernard Rudofsky, the Austrian architect and designer, who was at the
college for two weeks in August. At the time he was organizing the
exhibition Are Clothes Modern? for the Museum of Modern Art
(November 28, 1944-March 4, 1945), and his course and community
lectures drew from that material. His lectures, entitled: ‘‘How Can People
Expect to Have Good Architecture When They Wear Such Clothes?"’ and
 “The Unfashionable Human Body," included a look at the history of
 clothing as well as at ‘‘man’s unwillingness to accept the anatomic form
of the human body as satisfactory and definite.'' He described contem-
‘porary dress as ‘anachronistic, irrational, impractical, harmful... dictating
our behavior, dominating and conditioning all phases of life.''”? His stu-
_dents long remembered the absurdities he exposed, such as the number
 of buttons on a fully dressed man, the number of pockets, the layers of
 fabric around his girth, or the fact that a man wearing a shirt with a
 collar and a tie has innumerable layers of cloth protecting his neck while
an inch lower only one layer of cloth warms his throat. Rudofsky's
wife Berta taught an “impromptu” course in sandal making, which
was so popular that she was asked to repeat it the following summer.
The Rudofskys later formed a successful shoe-making venture,
Bernardo Sandals.

The nature of art, art and technology, and art education were a few of
the topics discussed by the guest faculty. The lecturers had in common a
belief that significant art springs from the spirit of man and is more than
 a technical exercise or a commodity to be bought and sold. J. B.
‘Neumann, director of the New Art Circle in New York, one of the few
galleries to exhibit the art of the Geometric Abstractionists, taught a
 two-week course in art appreciation. He defined art as ‘’an expression
of the spirit of man,'’ using as an example Albers's art, which he de-
 scribed as ‘‘mathematics with a soul, creations of an architectural mind,
 a play with space and color producing rhythm, emotion put into the ice
box, logic with a heart.'’ Charlot similarly described Albers's work as ‘’a
lifting of the veils...a getting at the spirit'’ rather than an attempt to
‘imitate nature. Ozenfant cautioned the students that ‘‘art is not a fragile
flower, nor is it a department of fashion; neither is it a distraction nor a
‘difficult, nor an easy hobby.''”?

 Other speakers opposed a romantic view of the arts and discussed the
 relationship between technology and art. In his lectures on postwar
  building, Gropius pointed out that the problems were both technical and
  social, the need for the ‘‘all-important creation of properly sized
| neighborhood units to serve as basic organisms for reactivating social
  intercourse.'’ He spoke against the ‘reactionary trend of thinking about
  the machine as an anti-human influence" and argued that it should be
  seen as ‘‘the modern vehicle of form'’ which man must ‘‘humanize.. . to
  give it social purpose by directing our energies towards the reconstruc-
  tion of our inner world.'’ Ozenfant agreed that it was a mistake to see
 “industrial, mechanical, technical and scientific knowledge as regrettably
 antagonistic to art,'' and the photographers repeated this theme in their
 lectures on photography as an art form. Josef Breitenbach noted that ‘’a
 good photograph...conveys insight, cuts the veil of misunderstanding,
 prejudice, and pettiness and gives us a glimpse of the truth underlying
 outer appearance’’; and Barbara Morgan listed as essential in the making
 of a photograph ‘‘the functioning inseparately of the camera lens, the
 eye, and insight.''”4

 Art education was an important theme because of the large number of
 teachers present. Ozenfant lamented the perpetuation of the romantic

|
 Var's End




  The end of the war and a resignation were catalysts for changes in the
’ Black Mountain community. In April 1945 Robert Wunsch took his last
  Black Mountain production, Tennessee Williams's Landscape with Figures
 (This Property Is Condemned) to the Carolina Dramatic Festival in
 Chapel Hill. In June Wunsch was arrested near Asheville and charged
  with “‘crimes against nature.'’ No one at the college was aware of any
* homosexual relationships and everyone was in shock. The arrest was
  front-page news in the Asheville papers, and the charge was a serious
  one and carried a prison sentence. Ted Dreier, who was on sabbatical in
  Cambridge, was called back to the college, and efforts were made to
  have the charge reduced. Although there is no known record of the
’ negotiations, the charge was changed to ‘‘forcible trespass,'’ and
  Wunsch agreed to leave the area. When released from jail, he returned
  to the college in the night to pack his few belongings. With his silent
 departure, the college lost one of its most devoted and idealistic friends.
  A "Louisville Fund’’ was set up to help him financially, and the faculty
  took a cut in salary to pay him the equivalent of a year's sabbatical sal-
  ary. After a rest at his home in Louisiana, he moved to the West Coast.
  He was last spotted at a performance in Los Angeles by a student who
  recalled that he had changed his name and was working for the post
| office. Wunsch failed to keep a meeting they scheduled.

' The announcement of the surrender of Germany brought both joy and
  sadness to Black Mountain. All classes were suspended the next day and
"the occasion was celebrated in the dining hall with a picnic supper and
  beer. Hansgirg gave a two-hour lecture on the splitting of the atom,
'which he defined ‘‘as greater than the invention of the wheel." Although
| most slept through it, Julia Feininger found it ‘'terrifying...a glimpse of
‘| what [destructive treatment] the whole construction of the universe is
‘| getting now from us humans." Two of the college's best students, Derek
Bovingdon and Roman Maciejczyk, had been killed in the war, and the
‘renewed communication with the European continent brought tragic
news to many of the refugees. On Sunday, August 14, Julia Feininger,
/ commemorated the war in her diary, ‘‘after dinner announcement at
 last, VJ Day, National Anthem, no words."'??

Reaffirmation




The resignations of Bentley, Cohen, Kahl, Foreman, de Graaff, and their
supporters in 1944 left the college with a drastically reduced faculty and
student body. In the fall only Josef and Anni Albers, Mac Wood, Molly
Gregory, Johanna and Heinrich Jalowetz, Gretel and Edward Lowinsky,
Robert Wunsch, Fritz Hansgirg, Herbert Miller, and Ted Dreier remained.
Fortunately, the faculty was able to quickly replenish its depleted ranks
with young Americans as well as European refugees, and veterans were
beginning to enroll as students. Among the most influential of the Ameri-
cans who taught during the postwar period were Mary Caroline (M. C.)
Richards in writing and literature; her husband Albert William (Bill) Levi
in social sciences and philosophy; Theodore Rondthaler, former principal
of Clemmons Consolidated School in Clemmons, North Carolina, in
Latin, history, and literature; John Wallen in psychology; and David
Corkran, former headmaster of the North Shore Country Day School in
Winnetka, Illinois, in American literature and history. Percy Hayes Baker,
on the faculty of Virginia State College, taught biology in the fall of
1945. History was taught by Robert Walcott, Jr.; social science and busi-
ness by Charles Bloomstein; economics by Karl Niebyl, Siegfried
Schwartz, and Tasker Howard, a Black Mountain graduate; and lan-
guages by Frank Rice, the son of John Rice, and by native speakers on
the faculty. Alice Rondthaler ran the office and taught shorthand and
typing. Immigrant faculty in the arts included Erwin Bodky in music,
Franziska Mayer and Trude Guermonprez in weaving, and llya
Bolotowsky in art.

The college was able to attract an exceptional faculty in science and
mathematics. Max Wilhelm Dehn, a noted Frankfurt geometer and stu-
dent of David Hilbert, was born in 1878 in Hamburg and received his
doctorate from the University of Géttingen in 1900. Assured of protec-
tion because of his professional eminence, Dehn had willingly given
academic openings in other countries to younger mathematicians; and
in 1938 he and his wife Toni were still in Frankfurt, where they were
living with a friend who was a judge. On Kristallnacht, November 9
and 10, 1938, when synagogues were burned and the windows of
Jewish businesses smashed, Dehn and his friend were arrested and taken
to the station where Jews were being loaded on trucks for deportation
to the concentration camps. The afternoon passed but the police who
knew the judge, did not call their names. In the end, the police an-
nounced that they could not load the trucks after working hours and
allowed them to go home. Dehn heeded the warning, and he and his
wife left Germany, miraculously escaping through the Scandinavian
countries, across Russia to Japan, and finally to the United States."

After teaching unhappily at the University of Idaho, the Illinois Institute
of Technology, and St. John's College, Dehn arrived at Black Mountain in
the winter of 1944 and remained on the faculty of his ‘‘beloved Black
Mountain” until his death in 1952. The landscape reminded him of the
Taunus Mountains in Germany, and the devoted hiker and botanist soon
knew the names and blooming periods of the wildflowers in the area.
Dehn often took his mathematics class up to the pasture and talked for
hours, exploring themes such as love, beauty, and death. As there were
few serious mathematics students, he tried to adapt to the situation by
teaching a course called Geometry for Artists, which left the students
completely baffled after the first few classes. It was a course in perspec-
tive geometry that dealt with classical relationships such as the Golden

      The most overt political challenge came through Karl Niebyl, an
     economist who was appointed to teach social sciences. Although most
      of the students were turned off by Niebyl’s doctrinaire approach to politi-
     cal issues and were generally amused at the few devotees who lustily
     sang the Commintern in the shower, he did gather a group of ‘‘ardent
      followers" who tried to indoctrinate other students and bring them into
      his group. The issue came to a head when the student body, under
      Niebyl’s influence, passed a resolution making membership in the South-
      ern Negro Youth Conference ‘‘binding on all members of the student
      body.'’ Some students felt it was a Communist-affiliated organization
     _and did not want to be members, and they fought the move. The faculty
     decided that the student body should have been more ‘‘concerned with
     ‘the protection of minority rights among the students" and asked that
     they reconsider the decision. The issue was resolved by having students
     join individually. At the end of his first year, the college decided not to
     renew Niebyl’s appointment. The general sentiment was expressed in a
     poem by M. C. Richards which opens with the line, ‘‘The way a man
     -eats is political.'"?

     |Many of the students felt the college was too removed from the critical
     social issues of the time. To assuage their consciences, a group led by
     Peter Nemenyi decided to have a weekly Mush Day on which simple
     food from the college's farm would be eaten and the money saved sent
     _to help those destitute in Europe. Participation was voluntary, and the
      cooks quickly became impatient with having two meals prepared simul-
     taneously. Beaumont and Nancy Newhall recalled that Nemenyi initially
     became upset because meals such as their tomato sauce, Ruth Asawa’s
     sweet and sour sauce, and Madame Goldowski’s borscht were superior
     _to the regular college fare and thus negated any sacrifice that might
      have been intended. He eventually came around and contributed his
1}
      own apple dish."*

  Undoubtedly the lack of a strong leader at the college in the postwar
  _ period contributed to the development of cliques. The discussions of
  educational policy were endless but rarely resulted in a consensus on
  _what the college should be doing. When Robert Wunsch was arrested in
    the summer of 1945, the faculty appointed Ted Dreier rector, although
  _he was on leave for the 1945-46 school year. In his absence, Josef Albers
 _ sat as chairman of the Board of Fellows and Herbert Miller as chairman
 _ of the faculty meetings. When Dreier assumed the rectorship in the fall
 _ of 1946, a deep-seated antagonism developed between him and Levi.
 _ Although Dreier had been an effective mediator and interpreter of the
 college ideals as a behind-the-scenes man, he was not a strong or effec-
__ tive leader. Wunsch had remarked earlier that Dreier tended to go ‘in
 _ fifty different kinds of circles'’ and that he was always ‘‘bursting with
    new ideas, some of them definitely contradictory to the ones he had
    day before yesterday."’ Wunsch had learned, however, that Dreier’s ideas
    were ‘'things to talk about, not to live by"’ and he respected his “‘earnest-
    ness and sincerity,'’ so they got along ‘‘famously."' It was not difficult for
    Levi, a man with ‘‘a mind like a steel trap,"’ to keep Dreier on the defen-
    sive, and finally, in the spring of 1947, Dreier gave way and resigned so
    that Levi could assume the rectorship."°

Bodman Fletcher, a graduate of the Harvard Graduate School of Design,

co-winners with Benjamin Thompson of the 1946 competition for a
dormitory for Smith College sponsored by Pencil Points magazine. In

Thompson, and John Harkness in forming The Architects Collaborative

with the expectation that a member of the group would be in residence
during any construction.

In March Fletcher visited for three weeks to make a preliminary survey
of the property, to determine long-range construction needs, to select
the site for a dormitory, and to discuss specifications for the building
with faculty and students. The visit generated a lot of enthusiasm, and
when Molly Gregory passed the hat for the construction program, she
collected $460. The program received a further impetus when an
anonymous donor gave $5,000. On his return to Cambridge, Fletcher
completed the site plans as well as the plans for a dormitory to accom-
modate forty women students. When the plans arrived for discussion,
Don Wight and other students, to the astonishment of the faculty, sub-
mitted an alternative plan for a dormitory combining sleeping and study
space for six students. The new plan represented a radical departure

116   An Essentially American Venture




Dahlberg recommended his friend Charles Olson to replace him in litera-
ture and writing. Born in 1910 in Worcester, Massachusetts, Olson re-
ceived his master's degree from Wesleyan College and studied for his
doctorate at Harvard University, where he also taught. After leaving
Harvard, he pursued a career in politics and public service until, following
the death of Roosevelt in 1945, he decided to leave politics and devote
himself to writing. At the time, Ezra Pound, whom he often visited at St.
Elizabeth's Hospital in Washington, was the primary literary influence on
his work. His reputation as a serious scholar and unorthodox historian
was established with the publication of his research on Melville as Cal/
Me Ishmael in 1947, and in February 1948, Caresse Crosby published his
first edition of poetry, Y&X, at the Black Sun Press. In the summer and
fall of 1947, he traveled to California to do research on the Donner Party
and in the Sutter-Marshall documents, and in 1948 he received a
Guggenheim fellowship for a book on ‘‘the morphology of the Americian
kultur,'’ a study of ‘‘the differing ways the Indian, white and the Negro
found out how to shape a human society in the West.'’ He soon was to
abandon this project to undertake a much more comprehensive task
encompassing the whole of contemporary knowledge, which was to
occupy him for the remainder of his life and result in several essays and
lecture series at Black Mountain.?°                                            Bill Levi and M. C. Richards. Photo-
                                                                               graph Eva Schlein Jungermann.
When the college approached Olson in the fall of 1948, he was not
eager to leave Washington, where he was working with a group of writ-          James Tite at the college press.
ers and dramatists. He agreed instead to commute to the college once a         Photograph Clemens Kalischer.
month for intensive seminars in literature and writing. For each session
he was paid travel expenses and $100. As his course descriptions indi-
cate, he, like Rice, regarded writing as a severe discipline and practiced
skill and as a process of coming to terms with one's beliefs and
 experience:

 Writing... The work is the exercise and practice of language by its two
 means, verse and prose, with the end that the individual learn to see,
 hear, feel, directly, to speak and think likewise (which is to write)....

 Reading...The work is the examination of writing, both verse and prose,
 with the end that the individual be led to comprehend the serious intent
 of the creative writer, whether he be Ezra Pound, William Faulkner,
 William Shakespeare, Homer, Seami or the writer who gives the
 COUrse....

 The act of the writer who teaches them is to help them to it by
 (1) learning them how to labor, (2) learning them the principle of
 intensification....

 It may, therefore, be also clear why the end is not to produce writers
 but men and women ofsome clarity and beauty (which is force). It is
 not impossible that a writer also be produced.*°

 The printing press was resurrected in 1946 and became an important
 part of the writing program. It was set up at one end of the woodwork-
 ing shop by three students, James Uimmie) Tite, Harry Weitzer, and Ann
 Mayer, who improved its efficiency with the addition of the motor from
 a ‘defunct faculty Kelvinator.'’ The students began to learn printing by
 trial and error and with the advice of a local printer. Their first project
 was a program for the spoof football game played on Thanksgiving

 1946 between the Cro-magnons (Prehistoric Specimens) and the Sticky
 Attitudes (Modern Neurotics) on a trapezoidal field with no parallel
 lines. In 1947 a second press, a Kluge platen press, was obtained from
 government surplus, and Robert Haas, who had taught at the college in
 1940, donated a complete font of Futura type. The printshop was super-
 vised by students Harry Weitzer (spring 1947), James Tite (spring 1947-
 summer 1948), Harry Holl (1947-48), and Warren (Pete) Jennerjahn
 (spring 1949), all of whom either had some previous experience in print-
 ing or learned the craft at the college. Frank Rice, who had studied with
 Albers when a Black Mountain student and had worked as an advertising
 typographer, supervised the printshop from the fall of 1947 through the
 fall of 1948. The students were able to print college bulletins and
 catalogues as well as administrative forms such as envelopes, question-
 naires, course cards, postcard mailers, letterhead stationery, transcript
 forms, and programs for concerts and drama productions. The various
 printings were charged to different departmental budgets, which showed
 that the printshop was paying its way.?”

ized the Cambridge Collegium Musicum. Bodky's curriculum included
such courses as Style and Structure in Music, Sonatas of Beethoven,
Development of Keyboard Music, Polyphony and Beethoven, and
Baroque Keyboard Music. His courses were illustrated with demonstra-

There was no formal dance teacher during the postwar years, although
students who had studied dance continued to organize informal groups.
In 1948-49 one group, directed by Elizabeth Schmitt Jennerjahn, created
its own dance-dramatization of The Lament for Ignatio Sanchez Mejias
by Federico Garcia Lorca after seeing a performance of Doris Humphrey's
interpretation of the poem. Jennerjahn, who was student-teacher in
dance for that year, had enrolled earlier to study art with Albers.
She left in 1945 to study dance in New York with Martha Graham and
returned to Black Mountain in the summer of 1948 to study with
Merce Cunningham.

In the fall of 1946, Josef and Anni Albers were granted their second
sabbatical. Albers went to New York until after his October exhibition at
the Egan Gallery. In an Asheville Citizen-Times article on the exhibition,
he was quoted as having remarked that he planned ‘to devote most of
[his] time to painting at a place where it is quiet, there isn't too much
education and not too many artists!"’ After the exhibition the Alberses
traveled first to the West Coast, then to New Mexico and Mexico. As
the end of the year approached, Albers was reluctant to return and re-
quested a second year away. He had been working intensely on his series
of paintings Variations on a Theme (also referred to as the Casa and
Adobe series), and he knew that his concentration would be broken by
the inevitable demands of teaching and community life. The faculty
agreed to extend the sabbatical through the fall semester but insisted
that he return for the spring to organize the 1948 summer session. He
spent the fall in New York, where he was ‘madly painting.''*°

 In Albers's absence Ilya Bolotowsky was appointed visiting instructor.
 Born in St. Petersburg in 1907, Bolotowsky was educated to follow
 in the footsteps of his father, who was a lawyer. His mother, who
 was an artist, encouraged him to paint, and after the family fled to
 Constantinople, he studied art at the College of St. Joseph. At the age
 of sixteen he moved with his family to New York, where he continued
 his studies in art at the National Academy of Design. He was employed
 by the Public Works Art Project (1934-35) and by the WPA Federal Art         Josef Albers, Variant ‘2 Light Grays
 Project (1935-41) and, like Albers, was a charter member of the Ameri-       & 2 Dark Grays against Blue,’ 1942-

 can Abstract Artists. During the war he was stationed in Nome, Alaska,

 as an instructor and translator of Russian.                                  Josef Albers Foundation.

 In February 1946 J. B. Neumann gave Bolotowsky his first postwar one-
 person exhibition at his New Art Circle. It turned out to be a traumatic
 experience, as his wife, from whom he was separated, slashed over
 thirty of the paintings. A change in scene was in order, and Neumann
 recommended him to Black Mountain. He was joined at the college the
 following summer by Meta Cohen. After a lecture on morals by Bill Levi,
 who discovered they were not yet married, they were whisked off to
 Asheville, where they were married on September 17, 1947.

 At the time Bolotowsky's painting was in a period of transition from
 the biomorphic forms he had used in his first abstract paintings to more
 linear, rigid geometric shapes. Although the tenets of Neo-Plasticism—
 flat planes of primary colors and black and white in a vertical and hori-
 zontal linear pattern—exerted a strong influence on his painting, he was
 not orthodox in his adherence to them. His Black Mountain paintings
 continued to incorporate curved lines, to use diagonals as well as pastels
 and colors other than the primaries, and to give the illusion of depth
 through overlapping. Although at first appearance his work and that of
 Albers seem similar, there were essential differences in their approaches.
 Unlike Albers, he was primarily interested in the plastic elements of
 the composition, and any optical effects, such as the illusion of depth,
 the interaction of color, and kinetic images, were only a secondary
 by-product of the painting.*°

By 1945 the college had become ‘‘a natural gravitational force’’ for those
interested in the arts, and both Albers and Bolotowsky taught an extra-
ordinary group of students. The artist Ray Johnson, one of several
graduates of Cass Technical High School in Detroit to attend Black Moun-
tain, heard about the college at the Saugatauk Summer Art School of
the Art Institute of Chicago through Elaine Schmitt Urbain, whose sister
Betty Jennerjahn had attended the 1945 Summer Art Institute and then
enrolled for the fall term. The San Francisco sculptor Ruth Asawa also
heard about the college through Elaine Urbain. Asawa, who had been in
a Japanese internment camp before attending college in Milwaukee,
first enrolled at Black Mountain for the summer program in 1946 and
then decided to remain. Robert Rauschenberg came to Black Mountain
from France, where he had been studying at the Académie Julian on the
GI Bill. Although he wrote on his application that he heard about the
college ‘‘through talk. Time Magazine. People who are attending Bard
College that did not like Blk. Mt.,'" undoubtedly Sue Weil, his future
wife, influenced his decision. She had visited the college before she left
for France, where they met, and was enrolled for the 1948 fall semester.
He applied in the fall of 1948 and entered mid-semester. One of the few
Carolinians to attend, Kenneth Noland first registered in the fall of 1946
under the Gl Bill. Though living in Asheville, he first heard about the
school through ‘‘National Weekly Magazines’’ and his brother Harry,
who was enrolled.”

Bolotowsky’s education had been in the beaux-arts tradition, and his
teaching method was more conventional than Albers's. His ‘‘fundamental
approach was one of permitting people to explore their own pos-
sibilities,'’ and, unlike Albers, he did not object to students copying the
styles of other artists. He gave individual and class critiques and was
known to send students to the library to look at the work of a particular
painter to see how he approached a similar artistic problem. In addition
to his classes in drawing and painting and tutorials in design, art history,
and criticism, he organized a film series of experimental and nonobjec-
tive films and arranged for exhibitions of gouaches and photographs of
paintings by members of the American Abstract Artists, etchings by
Stanley William Hayter and his students, pen and inks by Ben Zion,
gouaches by Alfred Maurer and George McNeil, and photographs by
Aaron Siskind, among others.?°

Bolotowsky was especially popular with the veterans and male students,
including Kenneth Noland, Joseph Fiore, Harry Holl, Gregory
Masurovsky, Knute Stiles, and Leo Krikorian. Unlike Albers, who was a
very private person—a student once admonished him that ‘‘though
‘good behavior results in good form,’ occasionally ‘bad behavior results
in a good time’ ''—Bolotowsky was himself a fun-loving veteran. He
was forty years old when he was at the college, had a black mustache
he frequently twirled and was always flirting with the girls. He would
cram as many of his ‘‘gang of rowdies’’ as possible into his car and take
them to drink beer and on trips to the mountains. Bolotowsky remem-
bered that the food was so horrible at the college that he used his salary
to eat in town. The students would buy hamburgers, and he would buy
a steak, which he would divide so that everyone had a bite. This was his
‘miracle of the loaves and the fishes.'’??

Bolotowsky was competitive and demanded loyalty from his students,
and when Albers returned after his sabbatical, there was a polarization
between the two men. Bolotowsky called Black Mountain ‘‘the outhouse
of the Bauhaus,’’ and Albers constantly had to deal with ‘‘rotating at-
tackers.'' At the same time, students recalled that Bolotowsky was de-
lightfully paranoid. He was convinced after Albers's return that he was
going to steal his paintings. He also feared that the Marxist economist
Karl Niebyl was plotting to lure him up a mountain road and kill him.*°

The Bolotowsky students who did take Albers's classes generally resented
his ‘‘Prussian'’ manner and found him regimented and pedantic. Some
felt he was too much of a ‘prima donna"' and resented his ‘‘virtuoso
performance” in class. Others who had ‘‘recently discovered, not only
painting, but paint and the sensuality of brush and paint and canvas and
turpentine’ and were eager to get on with the business of being artists
thought the exercises were silly. Ruth Asawa noted that Albers expected

all of his students to do the same exercises, whether they were Harvard
graduates or just out of high school. He ignored the work of students
who did not meet his expectations and could be very critical of those he
felt were not trying. Many of the Bolotowsky students accepted the
prevalent romantic image of the painter or sculptor as existing on a
higher plane than the designer or commercial artist, and a general criti-
cism of Albers was that he produced only designers and architects, a
patently untrue judgment.*"

Bolotowsky and Albers disagreed about student exhibitions, among
other things. Albers saw them as a reward for good work; he saw them
as ‘‘both a reward and a test."’ He felt that if a student's work was bad
and it was shown in the company of better work, it would be a proper
punishment and challenge to the student. Bolotowsky recalled that when
on Albers's return he mounted an exhibition of the work of his students,
Albers had a student keep varnishing and revarnishing the floor so that
no one could get in to see it. In another incident, Charles Boyce drew an
apple for the senior division examination in a spiral form with a wide-
edged pen. He recalled that Albers ‘‘attacked [him] for his incompe-
tence,'’ and Bolotowsky and his adherents came to his defense. A copy
of the drawing was posted on the bulletin board for days, and ‘‘sup-
porters and detractors pasted their mounting responses." Philosophical
and aesthetic opinions were supported by quotes from the greats, and
the debate finally ended with a four-letter word from Henry Miller. In
another instance, Harry Holl and Fritz Hansgirg, who were working on a
study of the physical characteristics of color, gave a slide demonstration
that contradicted some of Albers's theories about the mixing of colors in
light. Holl recalled that Albers stomped out of the presentation and that
the mimeographed copy of the lecture resulted in some students ques-
tioning Albers's theories and dropping his class.*?

Despite his long absence, Albers was not without his own loyal and
devoted followers, including Ray Johnson and Ruth Asawa, who felt
Bolotowsky’s classes lacked stimulation and challenge. Albers's teaching
was a continuous process not confined to class, and his excitement was
contagious. One day he picked up a discarded can of tomato juice that         Robert Rauschenberg with unicorn
had ‘‘a sort of virulent green mold” on the top and punctured it so that      costume created for his sister for

also observant of how students dressed and critical of sloppiness. He         Jalowetz-Aronson.
disliked the women wearing their shirttails out, as he felt that it broke

asked one student, ‘‘How can you make a beautiful drawing and then
wear this hideous garment?" Similarly, when a student stacked cases of
canned food behind a partition so that the cans extended over the top,
the word was passed to him from Albers that they disturbed the straight
line of the partition and would have to be restacked. Dorothy Ruddick
observed that there was ‘‘not only an intellectual tradition in him,
but...a sort of domestic tradition... you felt twenty generations of
grandmothers behind him and his approach.''*?

Even for students who found it difficult to study with Albers, his influ-
ence on their work has been tremendous. Robert Rauschenberg came to
Black Mountain because he felt he needed discipline and had read that
Albers was ‘'the greatest disciplinarian in the United States.'’ Albers
shared his self-evaluation, noting at the end of his first semester that in
painting he ‘‘could be better with more discipline" and that ‘‘with more
effort and concentration, [he] could have achieved better results’’ in
drawing. Apparently Rauschenberg found what he was seeking because
four months later Albers applauded his progress: ‘‘finally discovered that
intensive work and discipline are the means of development." In the
end, Rauschenberg generously assessed Albers as a teacher: ‘‘Albers was
a beautiful teacher and an impossible person....He wasn't easy to talk
to, and | found his criticism so excruciating and so devastating that |
never asked for it. Years later, though, I'm still learning what he taught
me, because what he taught had to do with the entire visual world... .|
consider Albers the most important teacher I've ever had, and I'm sure
he considered me one of his poorest students.''*4

                                       In addition to her teaching, Guermonprez executed designs for private

                                       based on a leaf motif created in part by a painted warp. She wrote of
                                       the technique:

                                       Pictorial weaving had been done mostly in the Gobelin technique,
                                       where the weft thread carried the color and formed the image. Often
                                       painters were the designers of these tapestries, and trained weavers hac
                                       executed them. My thought then was this: Painters used woven canvas
                                       as the base for their brushwork; why then should not I, as a weaver,
                                       enter the process at an earlier phase. | would paint on the warp and see
                                       how subsequently the perpendicular interlacing of the weft would alter
                                       color and texture.*”

                                       Guermonprez was a specialist in production weaving, and in 1947 she
                                       and Anni Albers proposed a production weaving program at the college
                                       Previously there had been no direct connection between the college anc
                                       the textile industry, although Anni Albers had sold her own designs for
                                       industrial production. The Board approved the plan on the condition
                                       that they raise the money to finance the operation. The program would
                                       have provided both for the development of designs that would be sold
                                       to industry and for the acceptance of commissions for custom designs t
                                       be woven at the college. On a trip to New York in the fall of 1948,
                                       Guermonprez obtained orders for production weaving; however, she
                                       recalled that the program which was terminated with her resignation in
                                       1949, had little chance for success because the Black Mountain student

                                       ing involved.*®

techniques, such as embroidery, knitting, braiding, and woven textiles,

                                     There was little change in the woodworking, bookbinding, and photog-
                                     raphy workshops after the war. After Molly Gregory's resignation in
                                     1947, the woodworking shop was supervised by Harry Holl, a student
                                     who had studied with José de Creeft. He was assisted by two other
                                     students, Nick Muzenic and Harry Weitzer. Weitzer and other students
                                     started turning out trays, bowls, salad spoons, forks, and other small
                                     items to see if the shop could be run as a small industry. Holl was also
                                     appointed student teacher in sculpture. An old shed near the woodwork-
                                     ing shop was transformed into a forging and sculpture shed, and a
                                     friendly tombstone carver in the next valley gave [them] a lot of material
                                     from his quarry.*?

                                     On February 3, 1946, the day following the sudden death of her hus-
                                     band, Johanna Jalowetz, who had taught voice and bookbinding as a
                                     tutor since 1939, was appointed to the faculty. Born in Czechoslovakia,
                                     she had studied voice in Olomouc and later in Vienna with Maria Gutheil
                                     Schroder and bookbinding in Cologne and New York. Besides her role as
                                     teacher, she was ‘Jewish mother" to the community, and her house was
                                     always open to students. Saturday afternoon tea at her cottage served
                                     during the Texaco opera broadcasts became a college tradition.

                                     In September 1948 fire destroyed the science building and the photog-
                                     raphy darkroom. Lost in the fire were many negatives of the work of
                                     Hazel Larsen Archer, one of the college's most gifted photography stu-
                                     dents, as well as Hansgirg’s magnesium plant. It was rumored that the
                                     fire was caused by Natasha Renner's vodka still.

                                     After the war, the faculty were disappointed in their attempts to attract
                                     an architect-in-residence, so they tried to provide interested students
                                     with some instruction during the summer sessions and with smaller build-
                                     ing projects. Finally several of the students—Paul Williams, Si Sillman,

Art as Experiment




The activities of the summer programs became increasingly interwoven
with the winter sessions. Many students who came for the summers
decided to remain for the regular sessions, and the energy engendered
during the summers had a tremendous influence on the winter pro-
grams. Furthermore, it was through the summer programs that the col-
lege was to begin the transition from an arts curriculum dominated by
the European tradition to one in which the ideas of young American
artists were to have an impact.

The 1946 Summer Art Institute was held July 2-August 28 along with a
regular summer session and work camp.°' Jacob Lawrence and Jean
Varda were both invited to teach painting for the entire summer.
Lawrence, whose series Migration of the Negro had been exhibited at
the Museum of Modern Art in 1944, was adjusting to civilian life after
service in the Coast Guard. He wrote to Albers that he would ‘‘conduct
a class in creative painting with the stress on individual approach to
‘subject matter’ "' and explained that if the artist ‘‘develop[s] an ap-
proach and philosophy about life.... he does not put paint on canvas, he
puts himself on canvas."' Albers wrote to Varda that Lawrence, ‘with his
subject matter—negro life—is on a somewhat different level compared
with you and me," which voiced both his conviction that abstract art is
a more advanced form and his eagerness to have painters whose work
was unlike his own. Interestingly, Lawrence's association with Albers
“reinforced his own already emerging tendencies toward abstraction.''??

Albers had met Varda, a Greek-born artist who had studied in France
and London before coming to the United States, several years earlier in
New York. Favorably impressed by collages in the November 1945 issue
of Arts & Architecture, Albers asked J. B. Neumann and James Laughlin
for their opinions of him as a summer-session teacher. Neumann warned,
“VERY CONFIDENTIAL Jean Varda is the most handsome looking man
you ever saw and the most perfect danger to every girl, therefore, not
so perfect as a teacher for your college. But if you need a ‘hengst' he
would be ideal."’ Similarly, Laughlin gave Albers reason for concern when
he wrote, ‘’Varda is a wonderful character. He is a saint, and also marvel-
ously entertaining. | calculate that his effect on your campus would be
something like that achieved by the Pied Piper of Hamlin. Varda can
enchant the bricks in the wall and make sane people believe that
Giorgione is all ‘mud and merde.' He goes barefoot in order to suck up
the good out of the ground. | love him.''92

Varda did not disappoint them. He arrived at the college in his Model A
convertible, which he had painted magenta and orange, after driving
from California with three spare tires and paintings for an exhibition tied
to the back. He had white hair and sparkling blue eyes, wore unlaced
shoes without socks (when he wore shoes at all), and had a broad
leather belt around his waist to hold his pants. He would throw packages
of Rit dye of different violent colors into the washing machine to dye his
shirts, which he wore open to the waist. For students who felt smothered
by the college's rather monastic atmosphere, he was like ‘‘a big breath
of fresh air... [the] great uninhibitor.'’ Mary Bowles recalled that Varda's
‘whole approach was not irreverent toward art in the least, but it was
full of fun and games,"’ and she compared his approach to Albers's: ‘‘It
wasn't this tremendously holy pursuit that Albers kind of layered over it.
| mean, with Albers you didn't laugh... you prayed, you knelt beseech-

142   An Essentially American Venture   ingly before the great god of capital A-R-T. And with Varda it was kind
                                        of a great explosion of the spirit...that one could do things, one could
                                        make mistakes, one could make a fool of himself and still have fun and
                                        still learn.'’ Varda was a ‘‘flamboyant, romantic and Bohemian" man
                                        who had ‘‘a kind of rhapsodic meeting of souls... with twenty people
                                        far into the night." His teaching made much of Greek mythology, and
                                        he talked constantly of the labyrinth of which we are all a part.
                                        As soon as he arrived, he hung his motto ‘‘To the inexplicable within and
                                        above us.''°*

                                        In addition to painting, there were classes and lectures in sculpture,
                                        graphic design, photography, architecture, art criticism, and the usual col- |
                                        lege curriculum. Sculpture was taught in July by Concetta Scaravaglione
                                        and in August by Leo Amino, who had come to the United States from
                                        Japan in 1929. Amino was still working primarily in wood, although he
                                        was beginning his pioneering experiments in the use of plastic as a
                                        sculptural medium. As there were no facilities for working with plastic at
                                        the college, he taught sculpting in wood using locust beams from an old
                                        building that had been torn down. Architecture students, disappointed
                                        that Gropius could visit only briefly for a lecture, organized their own
                                        discussion groups led by Peter Oberlander and Harry Seidler, two
                                        Harvard graduates who were enrolled as students. Bertrand Goldberg,
                                        who was designing an art building to be constructed at the college in
                                        memory of his wife, was also at the college for a visit in late August.
                                        Graphic design was taught in July by Will Burtin, the German-born and
                                        educated art director of Fortune magazine, and in August by Leo Lionni,
                                        the Dutch-born designer who was art director of N. W. Ayer & Son.
                                        Balcomb Greene, abstract painter and the first chairman of the American
                                        Abstract Artists, gave four lectures on ‘Trends in Art’’ in the last two
                                        weeks of July. Beaumont Newhall, who had recently resigned as curator
                                        of photography at the Museum of Modern Art, agreed to give four
                                        lectures on ‘'The History and Esthetics of Photography’’ during the last
                                        two weeks of August. The regular faculty rounded out the curriculum:
                                        design and color were taught by Albers, who was assisted in the labora-
                                        tory work by Alex Reed; weaving by Anni Albers and Franziska Mayer;
                                        and woodworking by Molly Gregory.?°

                                        The April 1946 issue of Design magazine, which was devoted to the
                                        1945 Summer Art Institute, brought over a hundred inquiries even before
                                        the summer announcement was mailed.?’ That plus the end of the war
                                        meant there were more art students at the college for the summer.
                                        Among the approximately sixty students were Harold Altman, Ruth
                                        Asawa, Lorna Blaine Halper, Dorothy Cole Ruddick, Joseph Fiore, Claire

                                        Sihvonen Loveless, John Urbain, and Don Wight. The fifteen work-camp
                                        students built an addition to the dining hall and raised the roof on the
                                        farm house to accommodate a second family. Charles Forberg, who had
                                        attended Harvard after leaving Black Mountain, returned to help clear
                                        the sites for the FHA buildings.

 were on sabbatical, and art was taught by the regular faculty. Beaumont

Fuller's greatest success for the summer was his portrayal of Baron
Medusa in the August 14 performance of Erik Satie’s Le Piége de Méduse
(The Ruse of Medusa), the culmination of the Amateur Festival of the
Music of Erik Satie. John Cage, who directed the Satie series, called it an
‘amateur festival’’ because at the time his knowledge of Satie’s music
was limited, although on a later trip to France he was to meet Satie and
collect more of his scores. During the summer Cage, assisted by Patsy
Lynch Wood and Richard Lippold, gave twenty-five thirty-minute con-
certs of the music of Satie after dinner on Monday, Wednesday, and
Friday evenings. Although some of the concerts were given in the dining
hall, the audience usually sat on the lawn outside Cage's cottage to
listen. At Albers's insistence, Cage preceded each concert with a ten-
minute introductory statement to familiarize those in the community,
                                                                                                                                                                                     ,
most of whom had been nurtured on the Germanic tradition in music,                                                                                                 SUVS ULSwSeSS   Ee”


with Satie's music and ideas. Ted Dreier noted in a letteras early as July10
that the festival was ‘‘slightly distressing'’ the music department.”?

The Cage concerts might have been dismissed as an amusing but trivial
entertainment had it not been for Cage's ‘‘Defense of Satie."’ In this
lecture, he stated ‘immediately and unequivocally, [that] Beethoven was
in error [in his definition of harmony as the basic structural element of
music composition], and his influence, which has been as extensive as it
is lamentable, has been deadening to the art of music." He explained                                 THE      RUSE       OF      MEDUSA

Cage had brought a copy of Le Piége de Méduse with him to the col-
lege; and M. C. Richards, who was in residence but not teaching for the
summer, translated it from the French. Although Helen Nickerson started
directing the play, she realized she did not understand it well enough to
direct effectively, so Arthur Penn took over. Fuller, who had reluctantly
accepted the role of Baron Medusa, had always considered himself too
self-conscious to act. To help him get over his inhibitions, Penn induced
him to join him in cavorting around the dining hall and then gradually to
work his way back into the role of Baron Medusa. Penn recalled the
preparation for the production:

| didn't know much more, | think, than Helen did, but | think | knew

time....we did break through an enormous personal shyness, which
was a terrific problem, particulary since he was playing the lead in a
play... [that was] for us, the first sort of communal atmosphere theater.

the community. Ray Johnson, who later founded the New York Corre-
spondence School, became a close friend and collaborator with Cage
and Lippold. Jim Herlihy recalled, however, that not all relationships
formed were productive. Isaac Rosenfeld, after reading a short story and
part of a novel Herlihy had shown to him, informed him that his writing
had no merit and that he should take an aptitude test to find out what
he could do well. He did, and the test said that he should be a writer.
Still discouraged, Herlihy left for the Pasadena Playhouse to study acting,
his second aptitude according to the test. There he wrote a play, and
once again found himself to be a writer.8*

Buckminster Fuller was recommended by Josef Albers to direct the 1949
Summer Institute. Fuller invited Jano and John Walley, Diana and Emerson
Woelffer, and Nataraj Vashi and Pra-Veena, all from the Institute of
Design in Chicago, to teach. John Walley taught the basic workshop and
Jano Walley taught ceramics and jewelry. Painting was taught by
Emerson Woelffer, and Nataraj Vashi taught Hindu dance and philosophy
and performed with his wife Pra-Veena. Three Black Mountain students—
Hazel Larsen Archer, Pete Jennerjahn, and Betty Schmitt Jennerjahn—
who were later to be appointed to the regular faculty, taught photog-
raphy, silkscreen, and dance, respectively. Diana Woelffer assisted Larsen
in her photography course. Marli Ehrmann, textile designer and weaver
at the Institute of Design, was invited by Anni Albers to teach weaving.
She had earlier visited the college and served as graduation examiner for

Fuller arrived at the college in June to get ready for the sessions. He
brought with him Lee Hukar, his secretary from the Institute of Design,
who transcribed his essay ‘Total Thinking,’' which he wrote at the col-
lege that summer. In his description of the summer program, Fuller called
for the education of the ‘comprehensive designer'’ who would do more
with less in collaboration with the ‘‘all-positive principle of industry,''
which, he noted, ‘‘is paradoxically being assimilated by man through the
emergent expedients adopted in emergency because of his preponderant
fixation in the direction of tradition."’ He observed that in general, ‘‘back-
ing up into his future man romantically appraises the emergent dorsal
sensations in negative parroting terms of his feudal misfortunes.''?4

Fuller and twelve of his Institute of Design students continued working
on an Autonomous Dwelling Facility within a Geodesic Structure that
they had begun the previous winter. The dome, ‘‘a tinker-toy-like hemi-
spherical structure of thirty-one great circles intercepting one another in
an all spherical triangular network" could be separated from the interior
living unit, which was designed so that it could be collapsed into a com-
pact form and moved. Only a model of the interior dwelling had been
made, but the dome—made of aircraft tubing laced with cable and
raised by tightening the cable, ‘‘almost as Ezekiel's dry bones must have
done’ —had been constructed and erected in the yard of the Pentagon

                                       bought cheesecloth in Asheville, dyed it beautiful colors, and made

                                       the unquestioning acceptance of the poetry of Olson and others, assem-

                                       Bible and ‘‘Father Albers's Notebooks," and gave a highly acclaimed
                                       performance.”°

                                       The exceptionally rainy weather in the summer of 1949 seemed to reflect
                                       the general atmosphere. The college itself was in a state of transition, as
                                       those who had decided to remain after the spring resignations of Josef
                                       and Anni Albers, Charlotte Schlesinger, Trude Guermonprez, and Ted
                                       Dreier were uncertain what the power structure would be or how this
                                       might effect the college's goals or their own positions at the college.
                                       Some were afraid that Fuller would seek an appointment to the regular
                                       faculty. Natasha Renner, an expert on corrosion, condemned Fuller for
                                       his use of aluminum and steel, which would corrode together in the
                                       dome. She was also critical of his method of measuring the strength of
                                       the dome—he would hang a desk on which four or five students would
                                       sit rather than doing mathematical calculations. By their very nature,
                                       Olson and Fuller, both compulsive talkers, were ill-suited for peaceful
                                       coexistence in so small a community. Although each man was looking
                                       for a comprehensive view of the twentieth-century world, Fuller's belief
                                       in technology as a solution to contemporary problems was anathema to
                                       the postmodernist position Olson was beginning to formulate. Fuller
                                       recalled that when he showed Olson his ‘Untitled Epic Poem on the
                                       History of Industrialization,'’ Olson was very excited; however, when
                                       Olson's former student Jonathan Williams published the poem as part of
                                       his Jargon series in 1962, Olson wrote to Williams, ‘‘And the other thing
                                       was yr horrifying news that you had anything to do with Buckminster
                                       Fller, and especially with that epic which he had brought out of safe to
                                       ask me to read that long ago back there in Old Carolina." Fuller noted
                                       that Olson read many of his poems, and he was convinced that Olson's
                                       line ‘‘Love is a verb'’ was a steal of his line ‘God is a verb"’ from his
                                       poem “'No More Secondhand God" (1940).74

' Gropius resigned from the Advisory Council. The students recalled that
  after the immediate crisis was over, Albers seemed joyous at last to be
_ relieved of the heavy responsibility he had carried for many years and

  Dreier left with his family mid-semester and the rest of the faculty left at
 the end of the spring term. The Alberses traveled to Mexico, where he
   gave a seminar in design at the University of Mexico. In the fall he gave
 _ aseminar and had a retrospective exhibition at the Cincinnati Art
" Museum. The following spring he taught a course in color at Pratt Insti-
* tute in Brooklyn, and in the summer of 1950 he taught design at the
   Graduate School of Design at Harvard. Although Gropius sought a
_ Harvard appointment, the Harvard administrators were unwilling to hire
 someone so close to retirement age to whom, because of his eminence,
_ they would have to give a full pension.'' Albers had been appointed to
* the council to reorganize the art department at Yale University in the fall
_ of 1948, and in 1950 he was appointed chairman of its newly formed
" Department of Design in the School of Fine Arts. Anni Albers worked
   independently as a designer of textiles, a printmaker, and an influential
  writer and critic. Trude Guermonprez joined Marguerite Wildenhain,
| whom she had known in Germany, at Pond Farm. She later moved to
  San Francisco, where she taught at the California College of Arts and
  Crafts in Oakland. Dreier returned to work at General Electric. By the
| end of the summer, Bodky was disillusioned with the new regime and
resigned to accept a teaching position at Brandeis University.

The remaining faculty were united only in their agreement that the
 |debacle of the previous year should not occur again. In the spring of
 1949, N. O. Pittinger was appointed special advisor, and on June 17 he
| was appointed rector effective July 1. At the same meeting the Board of
| Fellows—David Corkran, Natasha Renner, Theodore Rondthaler, and
, Raymond Trayer—passed a resolution giving Pittinger ‘‘unlimited power
| with regard to the reorganization of the College."’ The resolution further
_ Stated that Pittinger was ‘‘to formulate conditions under which he wishes
  to undertake the reorganization, with the understanding that the faculty
_ as a whole relinquishes its rights of participation in the administrative
  policy of the College."’ Thus Black Mountain College ended its sixteenth
  year having totally abdicated the right of the faculty to administer the
 college or to determine its educational policy or direction.'°7
