174.   A Community of Correspondences




Despite his dissatisfaction, Olson clearly identified with Black Mountain,
which he described as ‘‘Olson's University" and as his ‘'personal col-
lege.'’ He recognized the need for a leader who could bring the faculty
to a consensus and articulate a new vision for the community. Yet, unlike
Rice or Albers, who represented a ‘‘central intelligence,'’ Olson's leader-
ship took the form of a ‘‘single intelligence.'’ Olson ‘literally filled a
room, not only physically but by that dynamic energy,"’ and even dis-
counting his tremendous size—he was six feet and seven inches tall—he
was a man who psychologically could not ‘‘share his space."’ Like Apol-
lonius of Tyana, the subject of his dance-drama, ‘‘he craved to talk...to
get at things by talking about them....he was one of those who talked
to live'’ or, as he wrote to Creeley, ‘| damn well do talk to write."’ The
Black Mountain community was his audience and many proffered their
absolute allegiance. Dan Rice described him as ‘‘almost like a visionary"
and Jorge Fick as the one person who ‘‘could articulate the future."’ But
to Karen Karnes and others, his encouragement, which often took the
form of an ‘‘over-valuation of people'’—they were always the most
brilliant or most important writer, dancer, or artist—seemed to create an
“air of blownupness"' that was dangerous for the young students.'°

In the fall of 1953, Olson was appointed rector, the first person to accept
the position since the summer of 1949, and the faculty began its last
attempt at reorganization. Though a shrewd politician, Olson was not
an able administrator, as he acknowledged in the 1956 rector's report: ‘'I
am a great planner. | can ride ideas like a dolphin. And | have had to
learn to lay back from such things, in order to go on from day to day,
and from foot to foot.'’ He could make a heroic gesture when faced
with a crisis such as the loss of Gl Bill benefits or could formulate imag-
inative visions for the college, but he had no patience with the tedium
of administration. Wesley Huss commented that his approach was to
make a corrective or take a stance, but unfortunately at times he ‘‘over-
stood.'’ Although Huss and Hazel Archer, treasurers during the 1950s,         Stefan Wolpe and Hilda Morley.
                                                                              Photograph Clemens Kalischer.
were conscientious and competent, and Huss was loyal to Olson in much
the same way that Dreier had been to Rice and Albers, they lacked
                                                                              Grave of Max Dehn. Ceramic marker   -
Dreier's infectious enthusiasm and contacts and were no more able than        by Karen Karnes.
Olson to raise money.'®

The 1953 fall quarter opened with nine faculty— Olson, Huss, Fiore,
Karen Karnes, David Weinrib, Stefan Wolpe, Flola Shepard, Nell Rice,
and Doyle Jones, the farmer—and about fifteen students. Hazel Archer,
who had married a student, had opened a photographic studio in the
village of Black Mountain, and Natasha Renner, who also had married a
student, had moved to a nearby farm to grow mushrooms. To Olson
‘the place [was] more no-college now, and fast becoming a Chinese
monastery or hill-fort,"’ and Huss felt the college had become ‘‘a com-
munity of subsistence dwellers’’ with a faculty more interested in their
own work than in teaching. The dining hall and dormitories on the lower
property were closed, and the faculty and students moved into the cot-
tages on the hill. Students paid tuition and a fee for utilities and bought
and cooked their own food. Wood was burned in the fireplaces to heat
the cottages, and the college returned to the quarter system, closing for
the winter quarter from the end of November until the end of March to
save on fuel.'”

   In September 1955 the college signed a lease-purchase contract with
   George Pickering, who represented Eden Rock Park, Inc., for the lower
   property, including the lake. The contract for $65,500 provided for pay-
   ments of $2,000 on the signing of the contract and $13,000 on or
   before September 20, 1955; $10,600 on or before August 31, 1956; and
   $15,000 on or before August 31, 1957, with a purchase option for
   $24,900 in addition to all rental payments if exercised before August 31,
   1958. The first payment enabled the college to pay part of the accrued
   salary —the one-fourth unpaid salary since 1954—in amounts ranging
   from $150 to $700 to the faculty, who had only been receiving only a
   food allowance, and the second and third payments were scheduled to
pay mortgage notes due Paul Williams.??

  The fall quarter opened with the graduations of Michael Rumaker, Ed
   Dorn, and Jorge Fick. The faculty consisted of Olson, Wolpe, Huss, Fiore,
   Anthony Landreau, and Creeley; and the students included Isabel Voy)
   Aiken, Paul Alexander, Terence Burns, John Chamberlain, Dan Rice, and
   Jerry van de Wiele. Olson continued to be withdrawn, and in December
   he left for New York, where he remained until the spring quarter. At one
   point, he considered a satellite project whereby he would live in New
 - York and have a ‘‘weekend college’’ north of the city at the community
   where Cage, Tudor, Richards, Karnes, Weinrib, and the Williamses were
   living. The curriculum centered around Fiore's painting tutorials, Creeley's
   writing class, and Huss's theater activities. As often as not, Creeley had
   to be brought to class by students who found him at Peek's Tavern, the
   local beer bar and jukebox joint. Paul Alexander and Jerry van de Wiele        Dan Rice and Robert Creeley, 1955.
   recalled that class work was taken seriously, although Alexander also          Photograph Jonathan Williams.
   noted that parties often turned into drunken brawls. In December a
   group of faculty and students were arrested outside Peek’s. It was first
  charged that they had paid for the beer they were taking back to the
  college after closing hours, and when that charge did not hold, they
  were charged with ‘‘drunkenness."’ They claimed that Ma Peek was
  scheduled for a hearing and that it was deliberate harassment. Creeley,
  who was the first to acknowledge his difficulties, left the college in
   February for the West Coast.?*

  The 1956 winter and spring quarters brought new crises but also new
  life. Martin Sprengling, who was appointed to teach history in March,
  left soon after his arrival because he felt Olson had misled him in his
  description of the college program. Olson decided to separate from his
  wife Connie, and in March he returned to the college with Betty Kaiser
  and his son Charles Peter. He opened the spring quarter with a ten-day
   lecture series, his ‘Special View of History."'*? The poet Robert Duncan,
  who had spent the previous year in Palma de Mallorca, arrived in time
  to hear the lectures and to teach writing. The theater program was en-
  livened by his collaboration with Wes Huss. The woodworking shop was
   rented by Donald Mixon, a student, and the printshop to a former stu-
  dent, John Pike Grady.

  Despite the improved psychological climate, the faculty continued to be
  plagued by financial problems. The spring quarter opened with only
  tuition, the $1,000 from the lease-purchase agreement, and the $700
  rent from the farm due April 7 for operating expenses. In February a
  visiting official from the Veterans Administration found Huss to be the
  only faculty member at the college, and benefits were canceled as of

180   A Community of Correspondences




March 31. The other faculty, as well as some of the students, were in
New York. In May Olson organized a charade for a return visit by the
official. A course list was posted, students were dressed in shirts and ties,
and all moved in orderly fashion from landscape drawing on the dining
hall porch to French class and other courses. The necessary catalogues
were typed, course descriptions written, and in May the college received
provisional approval for students already enrolled.*°

The summer of 1956 brought new crises. Michael Rumaker, who re-
turned for a visit, recalled ‘‘a psychotic unpredictable energy in the air.”’
Two students who had prescriptions for speed and barbiturates intro-
duced drugs into college life. Another student had arrived with a woman
presumed to be his wife until his pregnant wife arrived to claim him. She
went to Travelers’ Aid for money to return home, and the college was
threatened with a morals charge. When investigators arrived to question
the student, he is reported to have replied, ‘Don’t pick on me, the rector
of the school is living with a woman." There was not enough money
and not enough people to take care of the property, and the buildings
were in a state of disrepair. The voracious kudzu vine threatened to bury
the college. In the music room records were melted in a Daliesque man-
ner, the library was in disorder, and the studies building was dank with
piles of trash in the studies.?”

For a second time the college made provision for another year by selling
land. In July the farm was sold to Wilma G. Miller for $35,000, with
$1,000 due on the signing of the contract; $9,000 on August 17, 1956
(of which $408.33 had already been paid in rent on the farm); and five

 In 1949 Hazel Archer was appointed the first full-time teacher of photog-
 raphy. She had studied at Black Mountain in the summer of 1944 and,
after graduating from college, returned to Black Mountain in 1945 as a
‘‘ graduate student" to study with Albers. She had been disabled by polio
as a child, and members of the community willingly carried her with
them to places she could not reach on crutches or in her wheelchair. Her
 photographs and especially her portraits are distinguished by their careful
composition and her sensitive perception of the individual, enhanced
 perhaps because of her immobility. As a teacher she emphasized the
 realization of the student's personal vision rather than experimentation
or the mechanics of photography. Photographers such as Henri Cartier-
 Bresson, Julia Margaret Cameron, Harry Callahan, and Aaron Siskind,
whose work demonstrated a strong formalist intent and personal vision,
were held in high esteem. In 1949-50 Archer and her students produced
a photographic publicity ‘‘viewbook"' and a photography journal, Five
Photographers, which was printed and bound at the college in an edition
of twenty-five. The journal, which appeared only once, contained state-
ments and individually printed photographs by Archer, Vernon Phillips,
Andrew Oates, Nick Cernovich, and Stan Vanderbeek.
                                                                               Hazel Larsen Archer. Photograph
After the college acquired a 16-millimeter Bolex movie camera, students        courtesy Hazel Archer.
began making moving pictures. The type of image that intrigued them
was a long shot of slowly moving objects, such as leaves on trees or the
movement of reflections on a pond. Andrew Oates, for example, made
a film of a willow tree and one of another student dancing at the lake.
Carroll Williams, Robert Rauschenberg, and Herb Roco each made a
three-minute, 16-millimeter ‘‘cameraless" film by painting the frames
individually. Rauschenberg's also contained live-action footage of Sue
Weil in Central Park.*?

Josef Albers had discouraged the teaching of ceramics because he felt
that clay, lacking the resistant properties of other materials, was too
easily abused by the beginning craftsman. Students, however, were
eager to have a ceramics program, and in the fall of 1949 Robert Turner
was appointed to teach on an instruction-production basis. After study-
ing to be a painter, Turner entered the College of Ceramics at Alfred
University, where he completed his master's degree in the spring of 1949.
When he was approached by Pittinger, he was looking for a place where
he could establish a production shop. After Turner's resignation at the
end of the 1951 spring semester, the pot shop was vacant until in the
summer of 1952 David Weinrib and Karen Karnes, both students at
Alfred, were hired. Though recent graduates, Turner, Karnes, and Weinrib
had all received recognition for their work at national exhibitions, includ-
ing the Ceramic Nationals at the Syracuse Musueum of Fine Arts
(Everson Museum of Art), the Young Americans exhibitions sponsored
by the American Craftsmen's Educational Counsel at the Gallery of
America House in New York, and the Biennial Exhibition of Textiles and
Ceramics at the Cranbrook Academy of Art in Michigan. America House,
which was a showcase for young craftsmen in the 1950s, gave Weinrib
and Karnes a two-person exhibition in 1953.°°

The potters, all three of whom hoped at the time to earn their living as
    production potters, received use of the college's facilities and room and
    board in exchange for teaching. They were charged for materials they
    used but were allowed to keep any income from sales. Using a loan
| from Turner, a gift from Turner's father, and some college funds, Paul
|



_ Williams designed and built a potshop in the field beyond the studies
  building. The shop, a concrete block and wooden structure with a work-
_ room of approximately 28 by 40 feet and a stoneware kiln with an oil
_ burner, had a large window with an exquisite view across the field to
_ the surrounding mountain range. A second workroom and packing shed
  were added by Jack Rice in the summer of 1953.

  At Black Mountain Turner worked with sculpted forms from which plas-
  ter casts could be made and with forms turned on the wheel. His pottery
  was functional and simple. Karnes worked almost exclusively on the
_ wheel, producing cups, casseroles, bowls, jam pots, plates, and other
containers. Weinrib, who soon found turning pottery to be too confin-
  ing, began to explore the potential of clay as a sculptural medium. He
  built his first slab pots at the college and created large tile panels which
  he decorated with images, primarily of animals. They showed the influ-
  ence of Assyrian cuneiform tablets and the glazed brick lions of the Ishtar
    Gate at Khorsabad as well as of archaic Greek and Etruscan ware.*"
    While at the college, he executed a commission for a tile panel for a
    house designed by Robert Orr, a former Black Mountain student, near
    the village of Black Mountain. The panel, adjacent to the living room
    fireplace, served to increase the heat efficiency of the fireplace.

    Turner, Weinrib, and Karnes were among the first generation of postwar
    American craftsmen whose task it was to reassert and redefine the role
    of the unique or handmade object in industrial society, to establish high
    standards of craftsmanship, and to create a market for handcrafted prod-
    ucts. Although the Bauhaus had successfully brought together the artist
    and craftsman to create a design aesthetic for the machine-produced
    object, increasingly the crafts had been relegated to the role of hand-         The pot shop. Designed by Paul
    maiden to industry or to a form of therapy. Trained in the university,          Williams in collaboration with

    In the fall of 1949, John McCandless was appointed to direct the
    printshop. At the time he was a partner in the Libertarian Press in Glen
    Gardner, New Jersey, a cooperative printing organization specializing in
    book and pamphlet work that had printed Robert Duncan's Poems
    1948-49 (1949). On a visit to the college to evaluate the potential of
    the printshop, he wrote that the press itself was ‘‘a fantastic bargain (my
    partners are thinking of becoming a college so they can get one)'’ and
    concluded that with minor additions the college should be able to do
    most of its printing.°? The following spring students printed the
    catalogue, the summer session announcement, the photography journal,
    and the postcard mailers in addition to the usual administrative forms
    and concert and drama programs. After McCandless's resignation in
    December 1950, there were several student printers who managed to
    keep the press running through the summer of 1953, when Carroll
    Williams, the student in charge of the press, left. In the summer of 1956,
    John Pike Grady, a former student, returned to rent the press as a com-
    mercial venture.

press and to handle administrative details such as distribution, but

accepting the position as publisher at the college could mean ‘'throwing
my lot in with his [Olson's] aims and those of Robert Creeley,'’ who had

Creeley, who was living in Palma de Mallorca, and Olson decided it was

dangerous step backward for the writers who had depended on it for
publication and because from the beginning Olson and Creeley had                                             The Black Mountain Review, Fall

would not only give them a guaranteed means of publication, but would
also bring publicity to the college and help attract students as well as
money. In December 1953 Creeley was appointed editor, and the seven
issues were edited from Mallorca, Black Mountain, Albuquerque, and
San Francisco, depending on where he was living at the time. The college
paid the printer and postage, but Creeley himself did not receive any
monetary compensation for his efforts.©4

Unlike Origin, which had as its epigraph ‘‘a quarterly for the creative’’
and printed primarily creative writing with a few critical essays by
Corman, The Black Mountain Review was to contain not only literary
criticism but also articles on what Duncan described as ‘‘serious dis-
course...about what is going on, what is the current state of data on
language, intelligence, time, the eye, the ear, the heart, the lungs etc.
which is all more vital at this point to the life of a writer than the
rationales of a taste for Eliot or for the Marquis de Sade.''©° In addition
to the poems, reviews, and other articles, each issue contained an eight-
page visual section with photographs, paintings, or other materials. The
64-page format in which the first four issues appeared was changed to a
format of 224 pages for the last three issues to accommodate longer
articles such as Carl Jung's essay ‘‘The Mass and the Individuation
Process'’ and Louis Zukofsky's ‘Bottom: on Shakespeare, Part Two."
Although Creeley had no difficulty in finding academic skimmers, he
could not find the type of serious discourse he hope to publish, and he
ended up writing many of the reviews and articles himself using
pseudonyms like Thomas White, Mauritius Esteban, WC, and AM. The
magazine's anti-academic stance was established in the first issue, which
contained articles critical of the two demogogues of the academic jour-
nals, Dylan Thomas and Theodore Roethke, an action which brought the
resignation of Kenneth Rexroth as contributing editor. The seventh issue
was published in the fall of 1957; and when funds were cut off, Creeley
was collecting materials for an eighth issue, which never appeared.

The most difficult problem facing the small publishers was distribution.

Although he was living in San Francisco, where Kenneth Rexroth was
the reigning guru, Duncan identified more closely with Olson, Creeley,
Levertov, and others working in the Pound—Williams tradition than
with the San Francisco Beat poets.

In January 1955 Duncan stopped at Black Mountain for a visit, and                 }



Olson read his recently completed ‘‘O'Ryan" poems. This was the sec-
ond visit for Duncan, who had stumbled on the college in the 1940s. In
the winter of 1956, Olson invited Duncan, who had been living on the
island of Mallorca and was running out of funds, to teach for the spring
and summer quarters before his fall 1956 appointment as assistant direc-
tor of the San Francisco Poetry Center. Duncan arrived in time to hear
Olson's ‘Special View of History’’ lectures and remained through the
summer. At the college he continued working on a series of poems
begun in Mallorca that was to be published as The Opening of the Field
as well as on the prologue and drawings for Letters (1958), which was
to be published by Jargon. Like Albers's drawing course, his workshop in
basic poetics focused on the elements of poetry: ‘‘Tone and Measure:
tone leading of vowels, consonant pattern, structure of rime; syllable,
word, syntactic phrase, breathing, line and verse as elements of measure
in composition by field. Stress and contour."'”"                                      Robert Duncan, 1956. Photograph
                                                                                      Jonathan Williams.
Hilda Morley, the wife of the composer Stefan Wolpe, was asked to
teach literature and Hebrew as a tutor when Olson was in Washington                   Hilda Morley. Photograph Clemens
in the fall of 1952. As a poet Morley feit so unappreciated because of                Kalischer.
both her gender and her literary interests that she escaped to New York
for the 1953 fall semester. She objected to the chauvinistic, patronizing
attitude toward women at the college during the 1950s and remarked
that the ‘faculty wives tended to fall into a background position, like a
minor women's chorus voicing the spirit of a limited consciousness in a
Greek play.''”? Her interest in T. S. Eliot, on whom she was writing her
dissertation and who was anathema to the Black Mountain writers, only
contributed to her feeling of isolation. Robert Hellman, a student at the
lowa Fiction Workshop, taught during the 1954 and 1955 summer quar-
ters. He had met Creeley in Europe, and Creeley had published his story
“The Quay" in the first issue of The Black Mountain Review.

Music during the 1950s was taught by Vollmer Hetherington, Margaret
Freeman, Lou Harrison, and Stefan Wolpe as well as by John Cage and
others during the summer sessions. In the fall of 1949 Hetherington, a
graduate of the New England Conservatory and Boston University, was
recommended by Erwin Bodky. His wife, Louise Hetherington, also a
graduate of the New England Conservatory, taught piano as a tutor.
Margaret Freeman, a graduate of Brown University and Smith College,
was appointed in the fall of 1949 to direct the chorus and a capella
group. The curriculum of the Hetheringtons and Freeman was conven-
tional, with courses in harmony, music appreciation, so/feggio, counter-
point, and composition. The Freemans left at the end of the 1949-50
school year, and Hetherington, although he had accepted a reappoint-
ment, resigned soon after the fall semester began when a salary cut was
announced. During the 1950-51 academic year, music was taught by
Johanna Jalowetz, Pete Jennerjahn, and Frank Moore, Olson's
Washington collaborator who enrolled for the fall term.

Lou Harrison, who had visited the college several times during the pre-
vious year, was appointed for the summer of 1951 and then asked to
remain in the fall. Born in 1917 in Portland, Oregon, Harrison moved to
California, where he studied with Howard Cooper, Henry Cowell, Arnold
Schoenberg, and Virgil Thomson. Later in New York he was a music critic
for the New York Herald Tribune, Modern Music Quarterly, View and
Listen and taught at Greenwich House Music School. When Cage recom-
mended him to Black Mountain, Harrison was recovering from a nervous
breakdown (his résumé stated simply, ‘‘lost mind'’),’? and Cage, who
had been helping care for him, was eager to find him a less stressful
situation than city life.

nature of the tableaux often blurred the lines between the performances
and community celebrations. For one party for which the theme of mur-
der and crime was chosen, the dining hall was transformed into a city
with streets, alleyways, and cabaret tables, and everyone came dressed
as gangsters. The bitterly cold January night was remembered by many.
As the party was starting, Rauschenberg, whom Olson observed ap-
peared to be “‘in a trance,’ danced through a wire screen porch, walked
further into the freezing waters of Lake Eden, and was dramatically
rescued by Twombly. For a medieval carnival there was a long street
lined with booths down the center of the dining hall and a fanfare, pro-
cessions, dances, jugglers, a play, music, and mime. Rauschenberg trans-
formed the stark interior of the dining hall into a jungle for another
party by hanging the abundant kudzu vines in the cavernous space.*?

Closely allied with the activities of the Light Sound Movement Workshop
were the productions directed by M. C. Richards. On her 1948 sabbatical
in France, she had translated Jean Cocteau's Knights of the Roundtable
and Marriage on the Eiffel Tower. She directed a reading of the former        June Rice Christensen as the Photo-
on October 22, 1949, and a performance of the latter for the 1950             grapher in Marriage on the Eiffel

                                                                              Photograph Andy Oates.
Richards directed a performance of William Butler Yeats's The Death of
Cuchulain, which was staged on the open gravel terrace of the studies
building beside the lake on ‘a windy, wild night.''®? Kerosene lamps
were used to light the performance area, and entrances were made
from the stairways leading from the upper floors and from the marsh,
from which the wailing queens emerged.

After the Jennerjahns left, the Light Sound Movement Workshop was
discontinued, although its techniques had repercussions throughout the
college's history. Katherine Litz, who taught for the summers of 1950
and 1951, was asked to remain for the 1951-52 academic year to teach
dance and to prepare Tim LaFarge for graduation the following summer.
Recommended to the college by Merce Cunningham, Litz had danced
as a soloist with the Humphrey-Weidman dance group and performed
with José Limon in The Happy Hypocrite and Reminiscence and in Agnes
de Mille's American Legend, Oklahoma, and Carousel. In the late 1940s
she began choreographing her own dances, which were performed in a
full-length program at the YM-YWHA in April 1950. Litz's Black Moun-
tain students included Timothy LaFarge; Nick Cernovich, who later pur-
sued a career as a lighting director for dance; and Viola Farber, who
danced with Merce Cunningham before forming her own dance com-
pany. She wrote of her approach to teaching that ‘‘the discovery of a
way to work is the most important factor to a dancer's point of view,
and a point of view is the most important factor in creative dance
development" and that her ‘greatest interest lies in the development of
the dance imagination peculiar and natural to the individual.'’ Her wit,
her beauty, and her dance combined to create a magical presence at the
increasingly male-dominated college.**

In the summer of 1951, Litz created two dances, The Glyph and Chorales
for Spring, both to scores by Lou Harrison, and in the fall The Long
Night, to music by Scarlatti, and Thoughts Out of Season, to music by
Morton Feldman. The Glyph, written as part of an exchange between
Litz, Lou Harrison, Ben Shahn, and Olson, became her most popular
dance. She also choreographed at least two dances for students     — Trans-
mutations (1952), to a score by Jay Watt, and Montage (1952), toa
score by Lou Harrison, both of which were first performed at the college
in March 1952. Litz's approach to choreography, which assumed that a
person's sense of movement is deeply rooted in the subconscious and
can be released through the process of discovery, had much in common
with the Surrealists and the automatism of the Abstract Expressionists.
The most effective of her dances, all of which achieved the distinctive
quality of a signature, were those that portrayed the personalities of
women through the slightest nuances of movement. Her sense of the
oblique and of the absurdity of the human condition, her lyricism, and
her unnerving sense of detachment made her later collaborations with

213   Art as Enactment




  In San Francisco in the fall and winter of 1956-57, Duncan and Huss
_ founded the Black Mountain Theater Project as one of the satellite pro-
  jects of the college. They began rehearsing Medea: The Will, the second
  play in the planned Medea trilogy, with Black Mountain students. The
  first act was completed and rehearsed, and by February the group was
  working on the second act. Huss and Duncan were both frustrated by
  the difficulty of achieving the intensity and coherence of the previous
  summer's work at Black Mountain, and Huss wrote to Olson, ‘‘My God
  what a definition of my desire—a large empty room with 15 people
  sitting in it.'" Most students were having to work at odd jobs during the
  day, and the city offered too many competing attractions for their atten-
  tion. Finally one of the central characters attempted suicide. As Duncan
  recalled, ‘He was in a crisis. | was feeding on the crisis toward the crisis
  of the character. And he just went completely to pieces, made a suicide
  attempt." In addition, the character Medea became so inextricably
  bound to the personality of Ann Simone, who played the role at the
  college and rehearsed with the group in San Francisco, that he later felt
  that the play could not be produced without her. After funds from the
  college for Huss’s salary were cut off and he began working for the
  American Friends Service Committee, the project was abandoned. The
  collapse of the San Francisco Theater Project and the publication of the
  final issue of The Black Mountain Review in the fall of 1957 marked the
  end of the formal curriculum of Black Mountain College.°?

Cage and Merce Cunningham returned for the first summer since 1948
to teach music and dance. They were also teaching in Burnsville, North
Carolina, for the summer program sponsored by the Woman's College of
the University of North Carolina in Greensboro. Since 1948 the work of
both Cage and Cunningham, like their reputations in the art world, had
changed radically. Inspired by his study of Zen Buddhism and his reading
of the | Ching, Cage had introduced chance methods of composition
into his music, which had alienated the critics as well as many of his
colleagues. Nataraj Vashi also returned for about four weeks to teach
dance. Jack Tworkov and Franz Kline, who were known to the faculty
and students through visits to the Cedar Tavern in New York, taught
painting in July and August, respectively. Si Sillman, a former Black
Mountain student who had become Albers's assistant at Yale, taught
color; and Charles Oscar, Litz's husband, taught drawing. Ceramics was
taught by Karen Karnes and David Weinrib. Lou Harrison, who had re-
ceived a Guggenheim fellowship in the spring, was working on his opera
Rapunzel, and Stefan Wolpe was invited as composer. A special course
in human ecology was taught by Edgar Taschdjian, a friend of Victor
Sprague and a member of the faculty at Loyola University. Taschdjian
also gave community lectures about hunger. William Joseph, a student,
was appointed to teach weaving.'°?

Tworkov, who taught in July, began his House of the Sun series, derived
from the Odyssey paintings on which he had been working in New
York. Although the major paintings were abstract, they evolved from
figurative studies that he explored simultaneously with the development
of the abstract paintings. Between Kline and Olson there was an im-
mediate and irreconcilable lack of rapport. Fielding Dawson later mused
that the core of the problem was Olson's inability, despite his size, to
dominate Kline, who was a successful rival for the attention of Olson's
students. Jorge Fick recalled that both men were centers and talkers and
that Kline did not want to get involved in Olson's rhetoric about the past
and the future. He noted that when Olson would start talking about
prehistoric man, Kline would say such things as, ‘‘Did you ever notice
how that car looks like a bakery truck?'’ He observed that whereas
Olson was interested in the ‘‘archetype of the white whale,” Kline was
interested in the ‘archetype of the B&O Railroad,"’ and while Olson was
talking about ideograms that could be made into words, Kline was creat-
ing ideograms that would become language. Typically, when Olson
wrote a poem to Cunningham, he entitled it ‘‘Merce of Egypt.''1°*

The activity that was to have the greatest impact on American art was
an experimental performance staged by John Cage in the dining hall.
Although at the time it was not considered especially significant, the
performance, later entitled Theater Piece No. 7, was subsequently recog-
nized as the first ‘‘Happening,’’ a seminal event in the development of
American theater. Cage recalled that he conceived the performance one
afternoon after lunch, and it was presented that evening. Each performer
was assigned a time bracket determined by chance procedures within
which he or she was to enact a particular activity. Although Cage had an
idea of what each person would do, specific assignments had not been

performance, a circumstance that is as much a measure of its success as
of the faulty memories of the faculty and students. Since the perfor-
mance was organized as a multi-focus event in which simultaneous,
unrelated activities would be taking place both in front of and around
the audience, each person's perception of the event depended on where
he or she was sitting and on what happened to attract his or her atten-
tion. When Johanna Jalowetz arrived early to get a good seat, Cage told

                                                                                 “Thoughts on Pitch."’ A theatrical farce, Occupe-toi de Brunhilde!, was

                                                                                 (1908), which Richards had seen either on stage or in the film version. A

                                                                                 England, he would be coming to the United States with Hamada and

                                                                                 Leach and, to a lesser degree, Hamada and Yanagi, were well known
                                                                                 among craftsmen in the United States. Through his work as a potter and
                                                                                 teacher at St. Ives in Cornwall and through The Potter's Book (1940),
                                                                                 Leach was immeasurably influential in raising the standards in ceramics
                                                                                 and in advancing technical knowledge for the potter. Born in China, he
                                                                                 had returned to the Far East after being educated in England. In Japan
                                                                                 he studied ceramics with Ogata Kenzan VI and met Yanagi, founder of
                                                                                 the Mingei Association to preserve the traditional folk crafts which were
                                                                                 being undermined by the industrialization and Westernization of Japan,
                                                                                 and Hamada, a young potter who returned with him to England and
                                                                                 helped him establish the pottery at St. Ives. In 1923 Hamada returned to
                                                                                 Japan, where he built his own pottery in Mashiko.

                                                                                 The leaders of the Dartington Hall conference did not reject the mass-
                                                                                 produced object nor did they suggest a return to the past. Rather they
                                                                                 sought to reinterpret the role of craftsmen in industrial society and to
                                                                                 learn how they might best be served by the discoveries of industry and
                                                                                 technology. Hamada and Leach, who had successfully established pro-
                                                                                 duction potteries that turned out thousands of pots weekly, had given
                                                                                 new dignity to the production potter through their superb craftsmanship
                                                                                 and through the breadth and integrity of their vision. On their transconti-
                                                                                 nental tour, the potters presented the concepts of Zen Buddhism and its

    The college had the ‘feeling of something that was running down in-
    stead of building up.'’ Some students were paying but others merely
    arrived, settled into a study, started attending classes, and eating in the
    dining hall, which made the paying students mad. There were so many
  _ empty studies that students would move from one to another leaving
    debris behind them. Rhodes remembered that the maintenance man
    had spilled acid on himself and couldn't work, and the cook was de-
    pressed and griped all the time because there was no money to buy
    food. Voulkos said he almost starved to death the first week because of
    the repeated appearance of slimy okra at the dinner table. A German
 _ museum director visited for a few days, and after he left, it was discov-
    ered that no one had given him sheets and he had been sleeping on a
_ dirty mattress. With the opening of the college in the fall, the enrollment
    was so low that the lower campus was closed, and the college moved
_ into the cottages on the hill.'?”

_ Every perceivable thing has form.


       Form can be either appearance or behavior.


       But since appearance is a result of behavior,

       and behavior produces appearance,


       every form has meaning.




- To understand the meaning of form,

_ that is conscious seeing of and feeling for form,

  is the indispensable preliminary condition for culture.


  JOSEF ALBERS, 1947

246   Epilogue: Continuations




                and Nick Cernovich, with whom they collaborated on many creative
                endeavors. Similarly, students were drawn to the creative community in
                San Francisco, where Ruth Asawa, Albert Lanier, Claude Stoller, and
                others settled. In 1948 Peggy Tolk Vaughan Watkins opened The Tin
                Angel on Sausalito's waterfront, where jazz musicians and folk singers
                gathered. Joe Fiore and Dan Rice painted ecclesiastical stained-glass
                designs on its doors and windows. In 1952 she opened a second Tin
                Angel on the Embarcadero, and later she has a third night club, The
                Fallen Angel. In about 1954 two other students, Leo Krikorian and Knute
                Stiles, opened The Place, the bar that was the gathering place for poets
                and painters of the San Francisco Renaissance. Although Duncan was a
                bridge between the writers of the San Francisco Renaissance and Olson,
                Creeley, and their students, the Black Mountain writers, with their em-
to
te
  tuscitiurté
  a22


                phasis on the particular and the craft of writing, provided a challenge
                and a counterpoint to the Beat poets, with their roots in mysticism and
                stream of consciousness.

                Beyond the extraordinary contributions to the arts by those who have
O               had stellar careers, there has been a more subtle and pervasive transmis-
uf)
                sion of Black Mountain energy and ideas into American culture through
                those who in less visible lives as homemakers, painters, musicians, col-
                lege professors, doctors, businessmen, bankers, administrators, pub-
                lishers, and writers have carried with them ideas and values that have
 a7
 §              influenced the patterns of their lives and of those around them. Further-
                more, for many who have had little specific knowledge of its history and
                accomplishments, Black Mountain College has stood as a symbol of
                academic freedom, of experimentation in the arts, and of the importance
                of the arts to American life. Founded in a period of economic depression
                and political totalitarianism, the college reaffirmed a belief in democratic
                government and individual freedom and responsibility. As with all experi-
                mental ventures, the college was always at risk. Its nature was mercurial,
                its spirit experimental, its setting modest. The process of learning was
                one of correspondence and conversation, and there was a concern with
                wholeness: the education of head, heart, and hand. Perceived as a field
                of forces, it was far more intense than a conventional educational institu-
                tion, and it is this energy released that continues to send vibrations
                throughout American cultural life.
